paper_title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.

Meanwhile, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures and can serve as interactive environments for agents. We study this intersection through the agent harness: the executable runtime that constructs an agents context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces budgets around models such as video generators. The report is organized around three directions. First, we study agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate script and shot planning, asset management, shot production, and editing, and we discuss what the evaluation of such systems must separate. Second, we examine agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state, including designs in which game engine or program written by coding agent holds the world state while the video model renders it, and where agents and world models test and improve one another. Third, we examine recursive self-improvement (RSI) for video model development: we separate revisions of current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the procedure that produces later updates, and we identify the channels through which an improvement could re-enter development. Across these directions, we analyze the agent capabilities that video imposes, from audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, and memory to interaction through code and computer use, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent organization. We conclude with open challenges, including autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance and cost accounting, and evaluation that links video quality and task performance to sustained improvement of models and harnesses. sections.title: 1.1 Motivation
sections.content: Video generators produce increasingly realistic, controllable, and temporally coherent clips [1]. generator alone, however, does not organize the decisions needed to complete video task. creative brief must become coherent shots; references must persist across scenes; takes must be inspected; edits must preserve what is correct [2, 3]. Interactive video must also support continuing actions grounded in observations, not just finished clip [4]. These requirements motivate transition from video generation to agentic video generation: goal-directed process in which generated results inform subsequent decisions. An agent can revise plan, retrieve reference, select tool, or localize failure in response to actual outcomes [5]. Agentic video generation denotes system-level perspective, not new generator architecture: the video model provides synthesis or predicted transitions, while the agent makes consequential choices around those capabilities. Video couples these choices over time. References affect later shots [6], actions change subsequent observations, and local repairs can disrupt temporal consistency elsewhere. Plausible footage may still violate narrative requirement or fail to realize an intended action, so quality score alone rarely specifies what to do next [7, 8]. Effective control requires connecting observations to localized decisions while maintaining project or interaction state and accounting for generation cost. The development from large language models (LLMs) to agents offers foundation for this control. Rather than only generating response, an LLM can operate within cycle of reasoning, tool use, and observation, as demonstrated by ReAct [9]. Planning and memory extend this cycle to tasks requiring multiple decisions [10]. Making these capabilities operational requires an agent harness: the executable runtime around the model that constructs its context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions and budgets [11, 12] (Section 2.2). For video generation, the harness is where creative brief or an interactive goal becomes executable operations on generators, editors, and world models. The central question shifts from generating good clip to reliably completing video task through feedback. Agentic video generation and video world-model interaction are two concrete settings. further question is whether experience from these tasks can improve the system that will perform future tasks. Feedback changes different objects at different timescales. Prompt revision or take replacement targets the current artifact [3]; retaining skill targets subsequent tasks [13]; updating dataset, critic, or generator targets later model versions [14]. These outcomes should not be conflated: effective repair of current video does not by itself establish improvement in future capability. Beyond repairing individual outputs, context engineering considers how instructions, retrieved evidence, memory, and execution records are selected and organized for subsequent decisions [11]. Agentic Context Engineering (ACE), for example, accumulates and revises structured context from execution feedback rather than updating model weights [15]. Such work shifts attention from current response toward reusable knowledge, while leaving open whether the mechanisms that construct and update that knowledge can themselves improve. Recent work on automated research extends these ideas to model development. The AI Scientist links idea generation, coding, experiments, and reporting [16]; autoresearch runs bounded loop of training code modification, experimentation, and validation-based acceptance [17]. These workflows connect proposals to empirical feedback, but automating fixed experiment loop is not the same as improving the loop itself. Research on self-improving agents, exemplified by the Darwin Gödel Machine and Regularized Recursive Self-Improvement (RRSI), explores changes to the agents own code or harness [18, 19]. Such work motivates examining the processes that generate and validate subsequent improvements. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) asks whether system can improve the procedures that produce further improvements [20, 21]. Video-specific targets include failure diagnosis, data collection, supervision construction, update selection, and candidate validation. Repeating fixed collection-and-training pipeline is iterative improvement. The recursive direction additionally allows evidence to revise that pipeline, changing how later round discovers and addresses weaknesses. An agent harness provides an executable surface for this direction. Its context construction, tool orchestration, memory, testing workflow, and update-selection rules can be inspected and, where authorized, revised [11]. This does not make every harness self-improving: revision must be retained and independently evaluated on later tasks or improvement rounds under stated resource constraints [19]. Figure 2: Agent involvement across three directions of video generation. Representative works branch from shared video generation foundation into agentic world modeling, agentic video generation, and development toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). These directions connect video models to sustained world interaction, coordinated production, and the improvement of models and the agent harness. Vertical position reflects increasing agent involvement, from No Agent through Agent Assistance and Agent Guided Improvement to Self Improvement. Existing video research supplies parts of this connection: feedback can revise reusable production skills [13], uncertainty can guide data acquisition for adaptation [22], and validation can govern critic renewal for later training [23]. These are building blocks rather than evidence that one system has completed the full RSI loop. Our survey therefore connects three questions: how harnesses organize agentic video generation, how they support video world-model interaction, and how they may drive video-generation development toward RSI. The first two establish task execution and sources of experience; the third examines persistent capability and the procedures used to improve it. Figure 2 maps representative work from shared video generation foundation into the three directions corresponding to the questions below.

sections.title: 1.2 Contributions and Positioning
sections.content: The survey addresses three questions about the influence of the agent harness on video generation (Figure 1), each corresponding to one core chapter. How does the agent harness enable agentic video generation? Agentic Video Generation (Section 3) studies how harnesses coordinate planning, execution, tool use, memory, editing, and watermarking around shared project state, and what the evaluation of such systems must separate. We examine how feedback changes generation and editing decisions and how those changes affect video quality, consistency, and efficiency. How can the agent harness be integrated into video world models? Agentic World Modeling (Section 4) locates where harness can intervene in observation, control, execution, event organization, and state management, and examines designs in which an engine holds the world state while the video model renders it. We examine how these interventions support sustained interaction, control fidelity, state continuity, and agent-driven evaluation. The focus of this question is how harness enables reliable interaction with video world model. 4 How can video generation systems move toward recursive self-improvement? Toward RSI in Video Generation (Section 5) examines how advances in video generators and the agent harness can feed back into the process that produces subsequent model improvements. We review foundation model improvement, agent harness improvement, and evaluation, and identify the channels through which gains in these components can strengthen failure diagnosis, data curation, training, and validation in later development rounds. The goal is to identify mechanisms and evidence needed for recursively improving development processes that can support next-generation video generation models. These questions connect through feedback: agentic video generation and world interaction can expose failures, while development can turn selected evidence into changes deployed in later tasks. Section 6 compares the shared agent capabilities that support all three settings. Differentiating Our Work from Existing Surveys Existing surveys provide complementary accounts of video generation. Work on spatiotemporal consistency examines generation models, representations, training strategies, and evaluation, emphasizing the mechanisms that maintain coherent video sequences [24]. Post-training and alignment surveys organize methods for adapting video generators to human intent, including supervised fine-tuning, distillation, preference optimization, and inference-time adaptation [25]. Evaluation surveys examine perceptual quality, semantic fidelity, and alignment with user instructions [7]. Together, these accounts explain how video models are built, improved, and assessed. More directly related to our system perspective, agentic visual generation surveys organize the conditioning, execution, and adaptation decisions available to controller across visual modalities [26], or study autonomous multimodal content creation and the construction of stateful artifacts [27, 28]. Wu et al. place agentic generation and world-modeling generation on single capability ladder of visual generation [29]. World model surveys characterize predictive and simulation capabilities across domains, focus on action conditioning, memory, and responsiveness in sustained interaction [30, 31], or treat world models as interactive proxies that supply feedback to continually improving agents [32]. Harness surveys analyze the execution layer around text and coding agents [12, 33]. Surveys of self-evolving agents and RSI examine evolutionary targets, adaptation stages, and feedback loops across general AI systems [20, 34, 35]. These perspectives share concepts such as feedback, memory, and agent control, but none of them takes the harness around video generator as the unit of analysis across production, interaction, and model development. Table 1 compares related surveys and adjacent studies by scope, thematic coverage (including RSI), and agent design. Our survey complements these perspectives with framework centered on video generation that covers three settings in which harness meets video model: as synthesizer in production, as an interactive environment, and as the object of development. The settings are linked through the harness: agents organize generation and refinement, while video models provide interactive experience that can inform agent decisions and further model development. Where capability ladders treat agentic generation and world modeling as successive stages of the generator [29], we take the agent harness around the generator as the unit of analysis, so that one framework covers production, interaction, and development. Our contributions are threefold. harness-centered framework. We define common agentharness execution loop (Section 2) and apply it to production, organized by workflow function (Section 3), and to world-model interaction, organized by the interfaces through which harness intervenes, including designs in which an engine or program holds the world state (Section 4). An account of improvement. We separate revisions of the current output from updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and from changes to the development procedure. We identify four channels through which an improvement could re-enter video development. No surveyed system yet revises the procedure that trains and validates the generator (Section 5). Evaluation requirements and open problems. We state how the agent harness supports active testing and reciprocal evaluation of agents and world models (Section 4.4), what the evaluation of agentic production must separate (Section 5.3), which capabilities video imposes on agents (Section 6), and which challenges remain (Section 7). 5 Table 1: Comparison with related surveys and studies. sections.title: 2 Foundations, Preliminaries, and Framework
sections.content: This section establishes the vocabulary needed to compare methods that were developed in different communities. We first describe video generation as conditional spatiotemporal modeling problem, abstracting away from particular generator family. We then separate the agent that makes decisions from the harness that executes them and from the models and tools on which it acts. We distinguish the roles of feedback-producing components, then formulate harness intervention across agentic video generation, world-model interaction, and model development toward RSI.

sections.content: Let video be sequence = (x1, . . . , xT ), optionally accompanied by synchronized audio. conditional video generator Gθ models pθ(x c, z), (1) where denotes one or more conditions and captures stochastic variation. The condition may contain text, reference images or clips, keyframes, masks, depth or pose signals, trajectories, camera parameters, audio, or actions. This formulation covers text-to-video, image-to-video, video continuation, video-to-video translation, inpainting, editing, and action-conditioned prediction. In an agentic system, is not necessarily supplied once by user: it can be constructed, decomposed, or revised by controller over multiple attempts. We first introduce diffusion and flow matching as generative formulations, then autoregressive video generation and its streaming execution, and finally video world models as functional role in interaction. These distinctions are not mutually exclusive model categories. Diffusion and score-based models learn to reverse corruption process, typically through repeated denoising steps. Video Diffusion Models extended this construction jointly across spatial and temporal dimensions [73]; later systems explored full-duration space-time generation and large-scale latent video diffusion [1, 74]. Most large systems operate in compressed latent space to reduce the cost of high-resolution synthesis [75], and transformer denoisers provide scalable alternative to U-Net backbones [76]. Flow matching learns time-dependent vector field, dxλ dλ = vθ(xλ, λ, c), (2) that transports samples from simple distribution to the data distribution; flow matching provides simulation-free objective for learning this field [77]. Here λ is continuous sampling time, distinct from the discrete interaction index used below. Autoregressive video generation factorizes generation into successive conditional predictions. Token-based models tokenize video, text, images, and sometimes audio, and write pθ(u c) = i=1 pθ(ui u<i, c), (3) where is discrete or continuous token sequence. Phenaki uses compressed causal video tokens for variable-length generation, while VideoPoet casts multiple video, image, text, and audio tasks into unified autoregressive interface [78, 79]. Such interfaces are attractive to harness because heterogeneous inputs and outputs can be expressed through common sequence model, although long sequences make planning and temporal state preservation difficult. Autoregressive temporal generation can also be combined with diffusion within each generated frame or chunk, as illustrated by Self Forcing [80]. For incremental execution, streaming generation produces and exposes successive frames or chunks before the complete video is available, rather than requiring full-clip output before execution can continue. It is an execution mode, not generative formulation mutually exclusive with diffusion, flow matching, or autoregression. Self Forcing demonstrates streaming autoregressive diffusion, and Matrix-Game 2.0 combines few-step autoregressive diffusion with action-conditioned streaming generation [80, 81]. For harness, incremental outputs provide opportunities to observe results and, where supported, update controls between generation intervals. This makes latency, temporal state retention, and the interval at which new control can take effect important interface properties; streaming output alone does not establish interactive control. 7 Video world models. For this survey, video world model is learned model of visual environmental dynamics that predicts future video observations from visual history and supported actions or controls [8, 82]. Using the same parameter notation θ, prediction over interaction steps can be written as xt+1:t+ pθ (cid:0) xt, α<t+, c(cid:1), (4) where indexes interaction time, α<t+ contains past controls and the proposed controls over the prediction horizon, and specifies additional conditions. Controls may be keyboard inputs, camera trajectories, robot commands, or learned latent actions. The world-model role extends synthesis to action-conditioned prediction or continuing interaction: returned frames can inform the next control or planning decision. long, plausible video alone does not establish this role. Neither an explicit 3D scene representation nor access to hidden state is required; control fidelity and continuity of interaction consequences must instead be verified empirically. Section 4 examines how harness organizes these capabilities into an interactive system. Across these formulations and execution modes, agenticity is determined by the decisions wrapped around or embedded within the generator, not by the choice of sampler alone. Video changes the design of an agentic loop in ways that image generation does not. Quality depends on both frame-level fidelity and cross-frame behavior, including identity preservation, motion plausibility, camera continuity, object permanence, causal ordering, audio synchronization, and long-horizon narrative state. Sampling and evaluation are expensive, single scalar score rarely identifies where failure occurs, and local repair can introduce downstream inconsistencies. These properties motivate hierarchical plans, persistent state, temporally localized critics, and budget-aware decisions about whether to accept, edit, extend, or regenerate candidate [7, 24]. The available interaction history is ht = (o0, a0, y0, f0, . . . , ot). controller policy πϕ specifies where At is the admissible action set, including termination when permitted. Agent Components. We use the functional decomposition Aϕ = (O, πϕ, M, , F), (6) covering observation, planning and decision-making, memory, tool-mediated action, and feedback. This is an organizing abstraction rather than mandatory module inventory: planning may be implicit in the policy, memory may be limited to the current history, and feedback may consist of returned observations rather than separate learned critic [10, 84]. plan structures future actions; the policy determines whether to follow or revise it as evidence arrives. The generator Gθ from Section 2.1 can be one tool in ; its parameters θ are distinct from the controller parameters ϕ when learned controller is used. Harness Engineering. functional agent description says what the system must do, but not how its decisions become reliable operations. For video generation, this requires coordinating observations, tool calls, and retained project state across successive decisions. An agent harness is the executable runtime that constructs controller context, exposes tool interfaces, dispatches and schedules operations, maintains state, routes feedback, and enforces permissions, budgets, and stopping rules [11, 12]. It is more than collection of prompts or tool list. It specifies, for example, which frames controller sees, how requested edit is applied, which artifact version is committed, and how failed operation returns to the decision loop. Delegation and background jobs, when supported, are further execution operations rather than prerequisites for being an agent. For this survey, we represent these responsibilities as = (O, C, , , M, F, R), (7) where constructs the controller context, executes actions, and determines admissible operations and termination conditions under task, resource, and permission constraints. O, M, , and realize the corresponding functional agent roles, with also committing updates to execution state. The agent and harness are thus not disjoint component inventories: the agent denotes the goal-directed decision process, while the harness implements and constrains its operation. Let st = (qt, mt, bt, et) be the harness-managed state before decision t. Here qt contains current task specifications, plans, artifacts, and their versions; mt contains stored evidence and experience, with its within-task or cross-task retention scope specified explicitly; bt records the remaining resource budget; and et contains tool and runtime records, including execution status, pending operations, timestamps, and newly available inputs. These boundaries also matter for attribution. Changing Gθ, πϕ, H, or the budget can each improve end-to-end results for different reasons. Runtime feedback may revise context, plan, or memory while leaving both θ and ϕ fixed. The harness specifies executable components and rules, whereas st records their current contents and execution state; updating st does not by itself establish persistent improvement across tasks. Human participation or reward signal alone does not imply agentic control or parameter learning [14]. Section 2.3 uses this shared notation to distinguish agentic video generation, world interaction, and persistent development updates.

sections.title: 3 Agentic Video Generation
sections.content: In agentic video generation, creative brief is developed into an edited audiovisual work through planning, shot production, and audiovisual editing (Figure 3). Scripts and shot specifications define the narrative and visual requirements; reusable assets guide the generation of candidate takes; and an editing timeline assembles the selected footage with narration and music. Decisions propagate across these artifacts: changing character reference may affect several shots, replacing take may alter the cut, and retiming the cut may require adjustments to the audio. Agents can participate at different stages by making production decisions, invoking tools, and inspecting intermediate results. The agent harness connects these activities and maintains the project state needed to revise decisions and coordinate changes across stages. Figure 3: Artifacts and revision in agentic video generation. Shot specifications lead to candidate takes and an edited audiovisual sequence. Shared assets support references, continuity, and version tracking; dashed arrows request revision. The final panel shows watermarking and provenance at delivery. The example is illustrative and not taken from surveyed system. We organize the literature by the workflow function system mainly serves: script and shot planning decides what will be filmed (Section 3.1); asset management keeps characters, scenes, and other references consistent across shots (Section 3.2); shot production creates the footage (Section 3.3); and editing and post-production assembles and modifies it (Section 3.4) and Section 3.5 covers watermarking and provenance at delivery. Asset management runs alongside the other three functions, which all read and update its records. Within each function, subcategories are separated by the object system mainly changes, and system covering several functions is placed by its main contribution.

sections.title: 3.1 Script and Shot Planning
sections.content: Planning turns brief into decisions that downstream tools can execute, at three levels of detail. Script development decides what happens: events, characters, and dialogue. Shot and task planning breaks the script into shot list and the tasks needed to realize it. Camera and staging decides how single shot is filmed: camera position, shot size, angle, and movement, and where actors stand and move (blocking). All three produce plans, recorded as text, trajectories, or engine camera objects; low-level camera control that conditions the generator belongs to shot production. revision at higher level affects more: changing an event can invalidate several scenes, whereas changing the camera keeps the story and assets intact. Script Development. MovieAgent [85] decomposes film into scenes and shots through hierarchical reasoning by production roles, keeping character, subtitle, and audio requirements attached to each shot. ScriptAgent [86] makes this intermediate representation explicit: scripter translates dialogue into cinematic script, and director uses it to coordinate generation with frame anchoring. MAViS [87] extends the plan across script, shots, characters, keyframes, animation, and audio through an ExploreExamineEnhance process. Co-Director [88] couples global exploration of creative directions with local multimodal self-refinement, and One Sentence, One Drama [89] combines story debate, spatially grounded references, and reviewers that target particular script 12 or visual failures. Both systems choose which narrative to realize before generating it. Selecting better take and rewriting the story should be evaluated separately, because the latter changes the target against which later footage is judged. Shot and Task Planning. AniMaker [90] connects storyboard to search over generated clip candidates; its photography and reviewer components evaluate each candidate in its story context. FilMaster [91] connects reference retrieval and cinematic planning to rough-cut-to-fine-cut process driven by simulated audience feedback. FRAMEWORKERS [92] plans production tasks rather than shot content: Director selects tasks and sub-agents from an editable Task Stack, and an Assistant executes them in shared Workspace that stores the resulting artifacts. Whether the plan is storyboard, retrieved shot plan, or task stack, writing it down lets failure be traced to the specification, the source material, or the generated candidate. Camera and Staging. FilmAgent [93] plans actor positions, actions, and camera setups in virtual set: directorscreenwriter critique corrects the script, and cinematographer debate followed by director judgment selects the camera setup before filming. Mind-of-Director [94] extends these decisions to 3D scene construction and character blocking and exposes the previsualization in an editable engine timeline. In both systems, staging decision becomes change to production environment that can be inspected before final rendering. Camera Artist [95] adds cinematography agent that specifies shot size, angle, and movement across shots; CamPilot [96] learns camera-work planning across consecutive shots; and AutoMV for real estate [97] plans camera trajectories alongside material, subtitles, and music. textual instruction such as slow dolly-in may be interpreted loosely by generator, whereas geometric trajectory or engine camera is executed exactly, so camera quality should be assessed on the form that is executed.

sections.title: 3.2 Asset Management
sections.content: Asset management links reusable material to the decisions that consume it. We distinguish asset creation, which produces new references; identity consistency, which keeps an entity recognizable across shots; and cross-shot continuity, which tracks the state that later shots must respect. Useful records include entity identity, scene membership, the time span in which an asset is valid, generation conditions, and dependencies on other assets. The main distinction is between stable reference and changing state: characters identity stays fixed while pose, location, or clothing changes, and each generation request needs the right combination. Asset Creation. Anim-Director [98] creates character and setting references, evaluates candidates, and uses the selected images to guide animation. MM-StoryAgent [99] prepares visual assets, narration, music, and sound effects with modality-specific agents that exchange structured messages. Replacing visual event can then require different sound effect, narration length, or musical cue. Creating assets thus involves choosing among candidates, and each audio asset must be tied to the scenes where it applies. Identity Consistency. AniME [100] places directors global memory above specialized agents and selects control conditions through MCP interfaces. MUSE [101] translates narrative intent into identity, spatial, and temporal constraints and uses multimodal verification to drive targeted revision. AutoMV for music videos [102] maintains character references, routes shots to narrative or singing-video tools, and regenerates or falls back when verifier fails shot. These systems differ in whether reference use is mediated by memory interface or by explicit constraints, but all must link the intended entity to the condition supplied to tool. Cross-shot Continuity. GroundShot [103] schedules shots by their usefulness as future references and verifies references extracted from generated footage before storing them, so an unreliable early shot does not become the basis for later ones; as result, generation order can differ from narrative order. MVAgent [104] separates persistent appearance references from the state observed at the end of shot and composes typed conditions for the next shot through observer, transition, and orchestrator agents. ViMax [2] combines hierarchical narrative retrieval with dependency-aware tracking of character and environment states. AgentMV [105] records references, segment dependencies, recurring motifs, costs, and execution history, and uses them to allocate song-level generation budget. Reusing an accepted motif saves generation call, but stale state or misaligned recurrence can propagate an error to every segment that reuses it. Keeping appearance, recent state, and narrative facts in separate records makes it less likely that visually similar but outdated reference is reused. Consistency Inside the Generator. Multi-shot generators offer different route to the same goal. Long Context Tuning [106] extends the attention of single-shot model to all shots in scene, with interleaved 3D position embeddings and asynchronous noise, so that shots can be generated jointly or extended one at time. HoloCine [107] generates whole scene at once, localizing each shots prompt through window cross-attention and keeping attention dense within shots but sparse between them, and reports persistent characters and scenes without external records. The two routes keep consistency in different places. In multi-shot generator it lives in the models context, so it needs no reference bookkeeping but is bounded by the scene the model can attend to. In harness it lives in explicit records, which can be inspected, corrected, and reused across scenes, and which allow one shot to be regenerated without touching the others; the cost is that every record must be supplied to the generator correctly.

sections.title: 3.3 Shot Production
sections.content: Shot production executes shot specification to obtain candidate footage. We distinguish three routes: model-based generation uses learned video generator; code-based animation writes programs, such as Manim scripts, that render the footage; and 3D scene and simulation builds spatial scene whose simulation or rendering produces the footage or conditions its generation. Model-based Generation. PhyT2V [108] refines prompts to improve physical plausibility, and GenMAC [109] coordinates design, verification, suggestion, and correction agents for compositional generation. SCMAPR [110] verifies rewritten prompts against their constraints before generation. VISTA [3] selects candidates by pairwise comparison and revises the next request from visual, audio, and contextual critiques, while VideoGen-Agent [5] learns to coordinate augmentation, generation, and verification tools over multiple interactions. In these systems, the controller can change how evidence is obtained as well as what is generated, and each revision must keep the requirements it does not target, such as identity and timing. MotionAgent [111] converts motion intent into object trajectories and camera parameters that condition the generator. Checking prompt catches omitted requirements, but only inspecting the generated take reveals failures introduced during synthesis. Many generation pipelines run as ComfyUI node graphs that agents construct and execute; these systems are discussed in Section 6. Code-based Animation. TheoremExplainAgent [112] turns explanation scenes into Manim animations and repairs code from execution errors. TeachMaster [113] adds debugging, synchronization, layout validation, and fallback after repeated rendering failures, and LASEV [114] coordinates solution, illustration, and narration agents through shared state. Code2Video [115] combines code repair with visual critic for layout problems, EvoPresent [116] refines presentation design with aesthetic feedback, and mPresenter [117] adds audienceoriented outline critique and compilerenderevaluate iteration. These checks catch different failures. Code that runs can still express an incorrect explanation, and correct narration can still be mistimed against the animation, so separate signals let the controller revise the responsible artifact. 3D Scene and Simulation. LiVER [118] arranges assets, lighting, and cameras in scene and uses the rendering as condition for synthesis, whereas MoReGen [119] renders the result of physical simulation directly. FantasyHSI [120] uses navigation, action planning, and critic to correct drift in humanscene interaction. Kubrick [121] iterates on Blender programs from reviewer observations, and GEST-Agent [122] checks scene-building operations against simulator state before execution. These three systems validate at different points: after generated motion, after rendered execution, or before an operation is accepted. Cutscene Agent [123] gives specialists MCP access to Unreal Engines cinematic tools, so local camera or animation change can be applied without discarding the rest of the scene. The benefit depends on how faithfully the tool interface exposes the engine and on which scene properties the agent can observe. When the scene keeps running and every frame is rendered from it, the generator becomes renderer of an explicit world state (Section 4.3).

sections.title: 3.4 Editing and Post-production
sections.content: Editing works on existing footage at two levels. At the sequence level, story-driven cutting decides which source intervals enter the cut and in what order, and timeline and tool execution carries out such decisions on timeline or media files. At the frame level, frame content editing changes pixels inside shot without moving it in the cut. We group semantic edits with restoration because both rewrite an existing shot and must leave 14 everything outside the target unchanged. At both levels, the editing state must keep source timecodes and applied operations so that revision touches only the intended interval. Story-driven Cutting. CutClaw [124] decomposes long source footage, anchors narrative to the music, and refines the cut with editor and reviewer agents. DIRECT [125] passes editing intent between screenwriter, director, and editor levels, and feedback can change the retrieval query and candidate shots. CineAgents [126] builds hierarchical narrative memory from source footage and develops creative blueprint into compiled sequence. The three systems differ in where the narrative anchor comes from: the music in CutClaw, an intent passed from screenwriter to editor in DIRECT, and memory built from the source footage in CineAgents. Timeline and Tool Execution. LAVE [127] translates user intentions into timeline operations within an interactive editor, while EditDuet [128] alternates editor actions with critic feedback in non-linear editing environment. In LAVE person guides the next action, and in EditDuet critic evaluates the evolving sequence; both rely on an explicit timeline whose state can be inspected after each operation. ELLMPEG [129] retrieves tool documentation and reflects on media-processing commands before executing them; valid command can still target the wrong interval, so the rendered output still needs inspection. Crayotter [130] stores blueprints, tool calls, intermediate renders, and exports as persistent artifacts, which supports failure diagnosis and resuming interrupted jobs. These records also let later revision recover why source interval was chosen and which downstream operations depend on it. Frame Content Editing. Aurora [131] uses tool-augmented agent to complete underspecified editing requests and construct conditions for video editing model. MMLVE-Agent [132] decomposes long footage and instructions by shot while tracking entities, so an edit reaches the intended occurrence of an entity. MAVFR [133] applies the same pattern to restoration: facial-detail and temporal-consistency agents propose toolchains that an evolving coordinator combines, and restoration results update the coordination memory for later tool choices. Both semantic edits and restoration must leave unaffected content intact, and the replacement must reach every timeline position that uses the shot.

sections.title: 3.5 Watermarking and Provenance
sections.content: Watermarks embed recoverable evidence in the media signal, and provenance records describe how an asset was derived. Where mark is inserted determines whether it covers generated take, an edited clip, or the final export. Generation-time methods need access to the generator: VideoShield [134] encodes information in the generation noise and localizes tampering by inversion, SIGMark [135] supports blind extraction robust to temporal disturbances, LVMark [136] learns marking within latent video diffusion model, and SPDMark [137] learns key-indexed parameter shifts that recover frame order. Post-production methods work on existing footage, including footage from closed generators: RBMark [138] embeds marks in wavelet coefficients without learned model, and SepVAMark [139] learns separable audiovisual marks for source tracing and deepfake detection. Detecting an alteration and locating it are separate capabilities, and robustness to compression says nothing about detecting unauthorized edits. C2PA Content Credentials [140] bind signed assertions about origin, ingredients, and edits to an asset. In agentic video generation, keyframe becomes an ingredient of clip and clip an ingredient of the cut, so locally regenerated shot needs its own identity and marking record.

sections.title: 4 Agentic World Modeling
sections.content: This chapter examines how an agent harness connects video generation to sustained world interaction. We first compare video generation models with interactive world models and describe their components (Section 4.1); then review semantic, state, and feedback mechanisms for agentic world modeling (Section 4.2), and systems in which an engine or program holds the world state while video model renders it (Section 4.3). Finally, we examine interaction reliability, active testing supported by the agent harness, and reciprocal evaluation of agents and world models (Section 4.4).

sections.title: 4.1 From Video Generation Models to Interactive World Models
sections.content: This chapter focuses on interactive world models built around video generation models as their predictive core. Both model visual content and its temporal evolution, and can use similar diffusion or autoregressive architectures. Conventional video generation usually produces visual sequence conditioned on text, images, or existing video, with emphasis on visual quality, condition adherence, and temporal consistency. Interactive world models use this capability for sustained interaction: they receive current observations and action conditions, predict the resulting changes, and return generated observations for subsequent interaction. The distinction lies primarily in how generation is organized and what it is used for. In an interactive world model, the consequences of an action need to remain reflected in subsequent steps, and generated observations must provide usable environmental information for the next action. direct path from video generation to interactive world modeling is to extend video continuation into ongoing prediction conditioned on actions. An initial image or video establishes the starting point, while user or agent supplies control signals during execution. The model generates subsequent frames or video segments under these controls and continues prediction from the updated context. This transition requires introducing action conditions, learning the relationship between actions and visual changes [141], and supporting continued generation. Genie [82], for example, learns latent actions to turn video prediction into generative environment with frame by frame control. GameNGen [142] predicts the next frame from past frames and player actions, demonstrating how video diffusion model can support interactive game simulation. These systems turn generation for describing or continuing visual content into environmental evolution driven by actions. Using the notation in Table 2, let αt be the control applied at interaction step and xt+1 the returned visual observation. The one step case of Eq. The returned observation extends the history available for the next control. Functionally, these world models connect current observations and state representations, action or instruction conditions, and the generation of subsequent visual observations. Current observations may be single image, recent video, or multiple views that represent the scene at the current interaction step. Control conditions may include keystrokes, camera poses, motion trajectories, robot actions, or natural language instructions interpreted by the model or control module. The predictive module combines these conditions with historical context to generate subsequent visual content, allowing the user or agent to assess the consequences of an action. State may be represented explicitly through objects, poses, and scene structure, or implicitly through video frames and latent features. Many video world models directly predict subsequent observations without separately exposing complete physical state. Predicting state evolution and generating visual observations are therefore often performed by the same model. This is functional decomposition, not requirement for separate networks or an accessible physical state. Sustained interaction also requires retaining information beyond the current view and finite context window. If an object has been moved, for example, that change should remain evident when the same region is revisited after leaving the field of view. Memory can supplement recent video context by storing and retrieving past scenes, spatial relations, and interaction outcomes to support subsequent prediction. WorldMem [143] stores historical frames with state information such as poses and timestamps in memory bank, then retrieves relevant content to support scene reconstruction. WorldPlay [144] reconstructs historical context so that earlier frames that remain geometrically relevant can continue to inform generation. These mechanisms extend the information available for interaction from recent video context to longer histories, supporting the 16 maintenance of world state. Implementations may use explicit memory banks, structured state, or latent representations; separate memory module is not required in every model. In embodied settings, video world models further predict the consequences of robot actions in physical environments, connecting visual generation to planning, policy learning, and control. UniSim [145] simulates the visual changes caused by high level instructions and low level controls, providing interactive experience for robot planning and policy learning. Cosmos [146] builds world foundation models through large scale video pretraining and adapts them through post training to physical tasks such as robotic manipulation. DreamZero [147] builds on pretrained video diffusion model to jointly predict future video and robot actions, forming world action model. These works illustrate different paths from predicting the visual consequences of actions to jointly modeling future observations and executable actions. Physical world models and world action models are thus closely related but not identical: the former emphasize predicting the evolution of physical environments, while the latter additionally incorporate action generation into the modeling process.

sections.title: 4.2 Harness Interventions
sections.content: Beyond relaying inputs and outputs, harness can organize the semantics, state information, and feedback on which continuing generation depends. We group these interventions into two families: semantic/event 17 mechanisms organize how subsequent changes are expressed; state/feedback mechanisms determine which history should continue to constrain generation and how deviations are handled. Both can be analyzed through the same sequence: world-model limitation intervention point mechanism evidenced system capability. The evidence for this layer is still thin: most mechanisms below are demonstrated in single system or proposed as designs, and few studies report gain attributable to the harness alone. Semantic and event interventions address the gap between high-level intent and executable generation conditions. request may describe desired interaction without identifying its target, preconditions, or event order. GameGen-X [148] provides model-side precursor through instruction tuning that connects user inputs to character behavior and scene content. LingBot-World 2.0 [4] adds VLM that interprets the current scene and user interactions before proposing subsequent events. More generally, harness can combine the current scene, user intent, and interaction history into event conditions with explicit objects and temporal relations. This changes the conditions received by the generator; rewriting prompt does not itself update the models dynamics. LingBot-World 2.0 [4] provides concrete example through its DirectorPilot framework. VLM interprets the scene and user interaction and proposes events, while the video generator realizes subsequent visual changes. The report distinguishes character-level semantic interaction, object interaction assisted by SAMbased tracking across video chunks, and textual world interventions that modify the environment or introduce entities. These mechanisms connect high-level intent to conditions for sustained generation. The interaction demonstrations support this system design; an isolated quantitative gain attributable to the harness is not reported. The corresponding questions concern whether control becomes more explicit and reliable: can target be specified consistently, does an event occur at an appropriate time, do its effects respect preceding interactions, and are actor actions kept distinct from world interventions? plausible VLM-generated event description is evidence about condition organization. Whether the video model realizes the intended transition must be judged from the resulting interaction. Semantic proposal quality and execution reliability are therefore separate properties. State and feedback interventions address the loss of historical constraints during long-horizon generation. WorldMem [143] motivates memory through the need to reconstruct scenes after long temporal or viewpoint gaps; WorldPlay [144] addresses the attenuation of geometrically important historical context. The current frame may omit an off-screen object, an earlier scene change, or an unfinished event. At the harness level, possible design maintains object records, scene summaries, and event logs; retrieves history relevant to the current interaction; and returns it through supported reference-frame, text, or state interfaces. Memory selects and transmits constraints. stored record provides effective state support only when the model can consume it and its subsequent generation is affected. External state management should be distinguished from model-side memory. WorldMem [143] stores historical frames with poses and timestamps, retrieves relevant memory units, and incorporates them into prediction through state-aware attention. WorldPlay [144] uses Reconstituted Context Memory to combine recent temporal context with spatially relevant historical video chunks, with temporal reframing preserving the influence of distant information. These are memory designs integrated with the generator, not generic external agent logs. At the harness level, tracking associates targets across observations, event logs record completed interactions, and retrieval selects information to return to the generator. These mechanisms may complement model-side memory, but cannot replace the models use of that information. LingBot-World 2.0 [4] likewise notes that long-term visual stability is not equivalent to true memory when revisiting regions outside the retained context. Feedback connects stored state to the next intervention. EVA [149] supplies concrete prediction-side example: its Reflection of Generation connects intermediate VLM reasoning with video prediction. Reflection about predicted trajectory should nevertheless be distinguished from selecting and executing an action in an online environment. More generally, harness can compare new frames with prior records, executed controls, and expected events to identify lost object references, unrealized events, or overwritten history. Depending on the available interfaces, it may retrieve additional history, narrow the next control conditions, request further observations, or re-execute from recoverable state. These are closed-loop design options, not uniform set of features already implemented by every surveyed system. Their benefit should appear as fewer subsequent 18 deviations, more reliable recovery, or more persistent state, rather than merely an explanation produced by checker. sections.title: 4.3 Explicit World State and Generative Rendering
sections.content: The interventions above leave world dynamics to the video model and improve the conditions it receives, so their effect depends on whether the model uses what it is given. different division of labor removes state and dynamics from the generator. game engine, simulator, or program written by coding agent holds the world state and applies its rules, and video model only turns the resulting coarse structure into realistic frames. Matrix-Game 4.0 [156] calls this design an executable game harness: lightweight game engine maintains the world state and executes interaction rules, and an autoregressive video model renders 19 the low-poly frames the engine produces. EdenLive [157] describes the same split, in which the upstream program executes the rules and maintains the world state, whereas the video model renders the resulting reference video. The generator is then renderer rather than simulator, and the program that holds the state acts as an environment whose state the harness can read and edit directly instead of estimating it from frames. Figure 5 summarizes this division of labor. Figure 5: Explicit world state and generative rendering. coding agent authors or revises world program that maintains state and applies interaction rules. Actions update program state, which an engine converts into proxy frames for the video generator. An appearance anchor and event text complement these structural conditions; proxy inspection can guide code revision (dashed). This division of labor is illustrated by EdenLive [157], SolarRenderer [158], and Code World Model [159]. Game scenes are conceptual illustrations, not outputs of these systems. What the structure fixes. The exported representation decides how much of each frame the engine specifies and how much the renderer must supply. Sparse layouts fix where things are but not what they look like: StreamRender-H3 [160] conditions on flat-color semantic maps from browser game engine, and the Programmable World Model [161] on 3D oriented bounding boxes compiled into pixel-aligned conditions. Geometric proxies add shape, as in the white-box frames that Magpie [162] receives from Unreal Engine, the low-poly frames of Matrix-Game 4.0, the coarse 3D simulations behind Coarse-to-Real [163], and the depth or surface normals used by AgentGarten [164]. G-buffers also carry material channels and leave mainly lighting and fine appearance to the model [165167]. Most of these renderers are trained for the representation their engine exports, so new engine or new kind of proxy requires new renderer. Two exceptions loosen this coupling: Code Video Model [168] conditions frozen generator on proxy renders without training, and SolarRenderer [158] passes untyped structural videos through the reference pathway of frozen backbone with single control LoRA and evaluates on representations absent from its training data. Where the agent acts. Placing an agent upstream of the renderer raises the question of when it is consulted. In Code World Model [159], coding agent reasons about events and writes the code that maintains the world state, after which deterministic per-step updates run without invoking the agent; its reasoning is spent on authoring the rules, not on producing every frame. The Programmable World Model instead translates natural-language instructions into programs for lightweight engine, and Matrix-Game 4.0 uses multimodal coding agent to turn players ideas into game code, so that scenes and gameplay can be created and modified in natural language. AgentGarten, EdenLive, and Code Video Model use an agent to build the world or scene before rendering, and the World Narrative Model [169] constructs an editable physical world with layouts, motion, cameras, and lighting before synthesis rather than during continuous interaction. In all of these designs the interfaces of Section 4.1 change form. An intervention becomes an edit to program state or rules rather than prompt or an action code, the observation interface can read state from the program instead of estimating it from frames, and objects outside the view persist regardless of how much context the generator retains. What the agent produces. An agent upstream of the renderer produces three inputs rather than one. The first is world program that fixes geometry, motion, and camera. Code World Model starts from existing 20 game-engine code and composes reusable proxy primitives whose position, pose, layout, camera, and state markers are addressable parameters. The Programmable World Model recovers entities from reference image with 3D detector and writes their states, relations, interaction rules, event triggers, and objectives. EdenLive builds standalone Three.js games in stages that define the mechanics, the static scene, interactive behavior, and the interface, and Code Video Model writes one Three.js program per shot, computing mathematically defined dynamics such as double pendulum directly in code. The second input is an appearance anchor. Instead of describing appearance in code, most systems have an image model redraw the first proxy frame into realistic first frame, as in Code World Model, Code Video Model, EdenLive, and StreamRender-H3. The third is text that places events in time: the agent of Code World Model writes timed action scripts, the coding agent of Matrix-Game 4.0 writes dynamic scene captions that condition the renderer together with memory references, the engine of EdenLive emits caption for the salient events of each chunk, and an LLM agent annotates the training clips of StreamRender-H3 with timestamped narration. Structure, appearance, and event timing thus come from code, an image model, and language, and the renderer has to reconcile them. Checking the program before rendering. Because the world is program, many errors can be caught before any frame is synthesized. EdenLive runs each game with real input and checks the resulting state, repairing failed checks within fixed budget. AgentGarten evaluates test rollouts from several probe cameras, queries the engine for contact, collision clearance, and occlusion, and repairs faulty poses or unsupported structures. The World Narrative Model checks script syntax, runtime exceptions, collisions, and boundary conformance, and compares rendered depth and silhouettes against references, while Code Video Model renders keyframes into contact sheet and revises the program against the scene description. These checks inspect exact state through simulation or draft renders instead of judging generated video. They do not cover the final step, in which the renderer turns verified structure into pixels. Speed and supervision. With the engine holding the dynamics, the video model sets the frame rate, and the systems that report real-time rendering reach it through few-step distillation. Magpie reports compute-side rate of about 32 frames per second on one H100, AgentGarten over 35 frames per second on one H100 with four denoising steps, and EdenLive at least 24 frames per second on consumer GPU; AlayaRenderer-Flash [170] raises G-buffer renderer from 0.56 to 31.54 frames per second, whereas Streaming Code World Model [171] describes its four-step version as not yet real time. Frame rate does not determine responsiveness. Magpie reports an end-to-end response of about 1.55 seconds alongside its frame rate, whereas Matrix-Game 4.0, which renders four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps, reports 60 frames per second at 480p on one RTX 5090 with 112 milliseconds from key press to display. Training pairs involve trade-off between alignment and coverage. Recordings from an engine align every structural frame with its target, as in Magpies 300 hours of interactive Unreal Engine play, the aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs of Matrix-Game 4.0, and the synchronized RGB and G-buffer frames that Generative World Renderer captures from commercial games, but they cover only the engines they come from. Structure estimated from real video, as for part of AgentGartens depth and normal conditions or DiffusionRenderers G-buffers, covers more content but carries estimator errors and can differ from what an engine exports. Proxy2World [172] avoids authored proxyvideo pairs by learning from posed RGB-D video, and Code Video Model conditions frozen generator on proxy renders without additional training. Agent-built worlds also begin to supply data: EdenLive synthesizes coarse-to-fine training pairs from agent-built proxy videos, and the evaluation sets of the Programmable World Model, Code Video Model, and SolarRenderer are built from worlds or programs written by agents. What explicit state does not solve. Moving dynamics into program relocates several difficulties. The renderer still invents whatever the structure leaves open, such as materials, lighting, cloth, and fluids, and nothing in the geometry keeps that invented appearance the same when region is revisited. Coarse structure can be ambiguous, as Magpie notes for the depth of white-box frames. The output can also depart from the structure it was given, which makes adherence quantity to measure; SolarRenderer, for example, compares point tracks and edges of the rendered video against its structural input. Because the intended state is available in the program, the harness has reference against which adherence can be estimated at every rendering step, which generator that keeps its state internally does not provide. The world, finally, can express only what the program represents, and an event outside its rules requires new code or return to learned dynamics. How to combine programmed and learned dynamics within one world remains open (Section 7.3).

sections.title: 4.4 Evaluation in Agentic World Modeling
sections.content: From video quality to interaction reliability. Video world models inherit the requirements of video generation for visual quality, semantic alignment, and temporal coherence, but interaction additionally requires generated states to support subsequent actions. visually plausible video may still ignore input actions, forget prior states, or produce consequences that violate environmental rules. Evaluation must therefore extend beyond video clips under given conditions to state evolution under successive actions and the support these predictions provide for agent decisions. Following the evaluation framework of agentic world modeling [30], we organize these requirements along three dimensions: long horizon coherence, intervention sensitivity, and constraint consistency. Long horizon coherence concerns whether states and the consequences of past actions are maintained during sustained interaction. Intervention sensitivity asks whether changing an action induces directionally meaningful change in the outcome. Constraint consistency examines whether generated trajectories obey environmental rules. Together, these requirements shift attention from convincing images to reliable interaction outcomes. In video world models, exploration, revisits, and controlled interactions make these requirements concrete. Orbia [173], for example, uses controlled exploration and revisits to separately assess input preservation, the persistence of generated content, and whether different views depict single 3D scene. Such tests reveal failures that short video clips may conceal: model can generate plausible images from the current viewpoint yet alter objects, layouts, or spatial relations when returning to previously visited region. Intervention sensitivity can be tested by changing an action at single step under matched initial conditions and checking whether subsequent states respond according to its intended semantics. Constraint checks further assess whether these responses respect collision constraints, support relations, object properties, or task rules. Different images under different actions establish responsiveness, but correctness must also be judged against the expected consequences. Active evaluation supported by the agent harness. An agent harness can turn these requirements into goal directed active tests. With the world model held fixed, an agent selects actions according to the test objective, inspects returned observations, and adjusts subsequent controls to reach states that expose model failures. WorldScore [174] evaluates controllability, quality, and dynamics through sequences of next scene generation tasks, providing unified basis for evaluating world generation. PlayWorld [8] introduces multimodal Agent Players that pursue long horizon test objectives through sustained interaction, covering geometric consistency, interaction fidelity, and state evolution within and beyond the current field of view. Its motivation is that different models may require different action sequences to accomplish the same test objective. Adjusting actions based on observations, rather than fixing control sequence in advance, allows the test to accommodate each models interface and actual generated outcomes. In this process, the agent harness organizes test objectives, action execution, historical records, and outcome verification. Evaluation records should retain requested actions, executed controls, returned observations, and verification evidence to distinguish world state errors from interface limitations or testers failure to perform the intended operation. Comparisons across models require matched test objectives, controller configurations, and resource budgets, with necessary interface adaptations documented. The testers control authority must also be constrained. For example, external world edits must not directly manufacture outcomes that should arise through interaction with the model. If development feedback is used to adjust an external control policy, final evaluation also requires independent held out tasks. SCOPE [154] provides concrete example by separating development feedback from held out assessment and freezing the selected control policy before the latter begins. Reciprocal evaluation of agents and world models. The tests above treat the world model as the evaluation target, while the world model can conversely provide an environment for testing agents. This reciprocal role is already evident in embodied settings: agents probe the reliability of generated worlds through interaction, while generated worlds test agents perception, planning, and action capabilities across different scenes, objectives, and interaction conditions. SIMA 2 [175] conducts qualitative evaluations in held out environments generated by Genie 3, examining whether an agent trained in game environments can generalize to newly generated naturalistic and urban scenes. This illustrates the use of world models as environments for agent evaluation. Such reciprocal evaluation must distinguish world model reliability from agent capability. weaker agent may 22 fail to reach states that would reveal model defects, while incorrect state transitions may make ineffective actions appear successful. Task success in generated worlds therefore needs to be related to outcomes in independent environments. WorldArena [176] tests policies of different capabilities in world models controlled through actions and compares their task success rates with outcomes in the RoboTwin simulator, assessing the validity of world models as policy evaluators. This motivates paired comparisons: hold the agent and agent harness fixed while comparing different world models, then compare different agents under matched world model conditions. Reports should separately present state transition fidelity, task completion rates, and agreement in policy rankings, with independent simulators or real environments used for verification wherever possible. Such evaluation addresses two questions: whether generated worlds withstand interactive testing by agents, and whether the agent performance measured within them reflects actual task capability.

sections.title: 5 Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Video Generation
sections.content: Under the definition of Section 2.3, recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires validated change to the development procedure ρk that makes later rounds more effective. The video generation literature provides many mechanisms for improving generators and the agent systems that use them, together with emerging examples of persistent changes to parts of the development process. However, the systems surveyed here do not yet demonstrate that revised development procedure improves subsequent rounds of generator development. We organize the discussion around three perspectives: (i) Foundation Model Improvement examines data curation and model training; (ii) Agent Harness Improvement examines the planning, tool use, memory, and reusable procedures that organize generation and editing; and (iii) Evaluation examines the feedback used to propose updates and the evidence needed to validate their effects. Most existing methods update the development state ξk, including model parameters and retained harness components, under fixed procedure. Reusing an improved component to produce further updates can create feedback loop, but establishing RSI additionally requires evidence that the procedure producing those updates has itself improved. We examine this distinction within each perspective.

sections.title: 5.1 Foundation Model Improvement
sections.content: This subsection reviews approaches to improving video generation foundation models through two coupled components of model development: Data Curation and Model Training. As summarized in Figure 6, data curation determines the training data and supervision available to the model, while model training determines how these signals are used for optimization. We include established methods to characterize the interventions available to an improving system, and examine emerging agentic approaches according to which development decisions they automate or adapt. These decisions include selecting data, constructing supervision, refining data pipelines, and using evaluative feedback for model optimization. The distinction relevant to RSI is whether these interventions only change the data or model being developed, or also improve the procedures used to construct and validate later updates. 5.1.1 Data Curation Data curation improves the data and supervision available for training video generation models. We organize existing approaches into three categories: (i) Data Acquisition & Retrieval, which collects task-relevant data; (ii) Annotation & Synthesis, which constructs training supervision through annotation and synthetic data generation; and (iii) Data Refinement, which improves data quality through filtering and correction. Data Acquisition & Retrieval. Data acquisition and retrieval provide training samples that meet the varying requirements of video generation models. WebVid [177] collects millions of videotext pairs from the web, providing widely used data source for video generation. HD-VG-130M [178] constructs larger collection of high-definition videos for text-to-video generation. VideoUFO [179] identifies topics of interest from real user prompts and retrieves corresponding videos from YouTube to improve coverage of content requested by users.
