VC-Agent [181] uses feedback from users accepted samples and rejection reasons to update its filtering criteria for subsequent video retrieval. The resulting data are used to fine-tune CogVideoX [193]. These approaches connect acquisition to user demand and feedback. Related exploration-driven environment learning uses uncertainty to select which experience to acquire [22], illustrating how observed capability gaps can guide data collection. Annotation & Synthesis. Annotation and synthesis provide supervision for video generation models by annotating existing videos and generating synthetic training data. Panda-70M [182] generates candidate captions using multiple cross-modality teachers and selects the best through trained videotext retrieval model. ShareGPT4Video [183] compares consecutive keyframes to describe changes in actions and camera motion, producing detailed video captions for model training. Vidu S2-Avatar [184] employs multiple agents to generate and verify temporally ordered captions aligned with individual events. For synthetic data generation, PhysInOne [185] synthesizes videos covering diverse physical phenomena to improve the physical plausibility of video generation models. Follow-Your-Instruction [186] uses MLLM agents to construct 3D scenes, verify layouts across views, and plan temporal evolution, producing synthetic data for video model fine-tuning. Agent-built worlds provide another source of synthetic supervision (Section 4.3). Their programs expose scene structure and intended state, providing references for annotation and opportunities to target observed failures. EdenLive [157] synthesizes training pairs from agent-built proxy videos. When generated samples are repeatedly reused for training, however, errors and omissions can accumulate across rounds. Studies of recursive training show losses of distributional coverage, quality, or diversity under the settings they examine [217, 218]. The provenance and mixture of synthetic and real data therefore matter when evaluating whether later rounds benefit from generated supervision. Data Refinement. Data refinement improves the quality of video training data through filtering, correction, and quality assessment. OpenVid-1M [187] improves video training data through quality filtering and recaptioning. Koala-36M [188] introduces Video Training Suitability Score (VTSS) that combines multiple quality indicators to select videos suitable for model training. For interactive world models, SolarWM [219] converts 1.43 million clips from ten datasets into unified record of observations, metric camera geometry, captions, quality metadata, selection decisions, and provenance, and separates source processing from mixture construction, so that new training mixture can be defined by changing filtering criteria or sampling weights without reprocessing the sources. Ditto [189] uses an agent to generate editing instructions and filter synthetic video samples, together with denoising enhancement to improve data quality. JAVEdit [190] uses agents to diagnose failures in data generation pipelines, modify code, prompt templates, or pipeline settings, and retain validated fixes for subsequent tasks. 5.1.2 Model Training Model training develops and improves video generation capabilities through different learning and optimization strategies. We organize existing approaches into four categories: (i) Pre-training, which establishes general visual and temporal generation capabilities through large-scale training; (ii) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which adapts pretrained models using task-specific supervision; (iii) Reinforcement Learning & Reward Modeling, which leverages evaluative feedback to guide model optimization; and (iv) Distillation, which improves generation efficiency through knowledge transfer from teacher models. Pre-training. Pre-training establishes general visual and temporal generation capabilities through large-scale training, where training efficiency and data utilization are important considerations. Make-A-Video [191] leverages text-to-image priors and unpaired videos to learn video generation without paired textvideo data. Stable Video Diffusion [192] adopts staged training approach, starting from an image model and proceeding through video pre-training and high-quality fine-tuning. CogVideoX [193] accommodates videos of varying lengths and resolutions through progressive training and diffusion timestep sampling. HunyuanVideo [1] uses scaling experiments to guide model size and training token allocation. Wan [194] employs progressive imagevideo training from low to high resolutions to improve the efficiency and stability of large-scale video pre-training. Supervised Fine-Tuning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts pretrained video generation models using supervised data to improve video quality and learn specific motion or control capabilities. Tune-A-Video [195] adapts pretrained image diffusion model for video generation using single textvideo pair. AnimateDiff [196] trains reusable motion module that can be integrated into personalized image diffusion models. MotionDirector [197] separates appearance and motion learning to customize motion from reference videos without copying their appearance. VideoCrafter2 [198] selectively fine-tunes spatial modules with high-quality images to improve visual quality without degrading motion generation. VACE [199] introduces unified conditioning framework for adapting video models to diverse creation and editing tasks. DreamRunner [200] uses LLM planning to identify required motions, retrieves relevant reference videos, and performs test-time fine-tuning to learn corresponding motion priors. MotionAgent [111] combines motion fields constructed by an agent with fine-tuned optical flow adapter to enable precise motion control. Reinforcement Learning & Reward Modeling. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves video generation models by optimizing their parameters using reward signals. Reward modeling plays an important role in this process by learning to assess generated videos and provide rewards for optimization. Constructing reliable rewards requires considering multiple aspects of video quality, as well as the visual evidence and scoring criteria used for assessment. VideoScore [201] trains video quality assessment model on human annotations of visual quality, temporal consistency, and other evaluation dimensions. VideoReward [14] trains video reward model on multidimensional human preferences. RewardDance [202] shifts from regressive to generative reward modeling, aligning reward prediction with the VLMs next-token prediction objective, enabling more effective scaling across model size and input context. VR-Thinker [203] actively selects additional video frames during reasoning to gather visual evidence. RewardVerse [204] learns to generate task-specific rubrics for assessing video quality. The latter two improve reward modeling by refining the visual evidence considered and the criteria used to assess generated videos. Beyond constructing reliable reward signals, another important direction is how to leverage them to optimize video generation models. InstructVideo [205] uses image reward models to fine-tune video diffusion models, reformulating reward optimization as editing to reduce training costs. VideoDPO [206] constructs preference pairs from composite scores for offline preference optimization. DanceGRPO [207] incorporates rewards from VideoReward into GRPO to optimize the video generator. SPIRAL [208] incorporates agent feedback into multi-step action video generation: PlanAgent decomposes action goals, CriticAgent inspects generated video clips and triggers revisions, and the video generator is further optimized through GRPO using rewards from the critic. Dual-IPO [23] alternates improvements to the reward model and the generator. Such methods allow evaluators to shape the data and objectives used for generator optimization, making the reliability of 25 those evaluators development concern as well as an evaluation concern (Section 5.3). Distillation. Distillation transfers knowledge from teacher models to student models to improve video generation efficiency without substantially sacrificing generation quality. T2V-Turbo [209, 210] incorporates differentiable reward feedback into consistency distillation to improve video quality with fewer sampling steps. Motion Consistency Model [211] separates motion distillation from appearance enhancement, using high-quality image data to improve frame appearance without degrading temporal dynamics. Transition Matching Distillation (TMD) [212] approximates multi-step denoising trajectories using small number of probability transitions modeled by conditional flows. PDD [213] accelerates generation by predicting multiple denoising steps within each model evaluation, improving sampling efficiency and generation diversity. AnyFlow [214] learns flow map transitions over arbitrary time intervals, allowing distilled models to improve generation quality as more sampling steps become available. Distillation can also be used to train autoregressive video diffusion models, which generate video chunks sequentially through diffusion conditioned on previously generated content. CausVid [215] transfers knowledge from multi-step bidirectional diffusion teacher to few-step autoregressive student for faster video generation. Building on CausVid, Self Forcing [80] further trains the student on its own generated histories through autoregressive rollouts and video-level distribution matching to reduce the traininginference gap. Causal Forcing [216] addresses the architectural mismatch between bidirectional teachers and autoregressive students by using an autoregressive teacher to provide generation trajectories for student initialization, followed by distribution matching with the bidirectional teacher. Across data curation and model training, improved generators can provide supervision, improved evaluators can change which samples are selected, and production feedback can guide acquisition. These mechanisms connect model use to further development. They can nevertheless operate under fixed rules for collecting data, optimizing parameters, and accepting candidates. JAVEdit provides more direct example of persistent change to part of the development procedure by retaining validated pipeline fixes. The remaining question is whether such changes make later development rounds more effective, including their effects on training and candidate validation. This requires measuring the quality and cost of subsequent updates, beyond the quality of the data or model produced in the current round (Section 5.3).

sections.title: 5.2 Agent Harness Improvement
sections.content: The agent harness (Section 2.2) can play two roles in development. production harness organizes generation and editing for request; development harness diagnoses failures, curates data, launches training, and validates candidates. The components reviewed below belong mostly to production harnesses. Many of them revise only the current output; those that retain memory, rules, skills, or trained controller weights update ξk. These mechanisms also provide ways to organize development decisions. Their relevance to RSI depends on whether retained changes improve the procedures used to diagnose failures, construct updates, and validate later candidates. We review four functional components: (i) Planning & Orchestration, (ii) Tool Use & Control, (iii) Memory & Experience, and (iv) Skills & Reusable Procedures. Together, they cover production organization, individual operations, and the retention of evidence and methods for future use. Adaptation and training mechanisms are discussed separately at the end. 5.2.1 Planning & Orchestration Video production involves deciding what to produce, organizing execution, and responding to failures. Following these responsibilities, we review Production Planning, Execution Coordination, and Review & Recovery. Production Planning. Production planning translates request into creative specifications and structured production steps. MovieAgent [85] decomposes stories into scene and shot plans. Co-Director [88] explores creative configurations while revising storylines and keyframes. MultiMedia-Agent [220] addresses executable plans for multimedia production, while AgenticGen [221] connects advertising strategy selection to executable drafts. Methods are grouped by their primary contribution to planning and orchestration, tool use and control, memory and experience, or reusable procedures. steps. Execution Coordination. Execution coordination manages how tools and agents carry out plan, including action order and dependencies. VideoGen-Agent [5] organizes multi-turn tool use into production trajectories. NEWTON [222] uses planner to organize actions involving fixed generator, verifier, and toolset. Recommendation as Generation [223] connects instruction and video-agent policies within recommendation-oriented production under quality constraints. The inputs and controls for individual tool calls are discussed under Tool Use & Control. Review & Recovery. Review and recovery determines where feedback should be applied and which stages should be revisited when intermediate results are unsatisfactory. CHIEF [224] converts audience and film-critic feedback into revision requests, while CogenPVG [225] distributes generatorcritic pairs across argument, storyboard, asset, and editing stages. VideoAgent [226] changes the execution structure by correcting edges, adding missing nodes, and revising the order of an editing-agent DAG. CutClaw [124] backtracks to alternative footage intervals after review. These mechanisms direct revision within the workflow; the corrective operations themselves belong to the tool-use and editing interface. 5.2.2 Tool Use & Control Production plans must be translated into operations supported by available tools. We review Tool Selection & Conditioning for guiding generation, followed by Editing & Repair for correcting existing results. Tool Selection & Conditioning. Tool selection and conditioning matches production requirement to generator and expresses it through prompts, references, and other control inputs. SPAgent [227] evaluates newly introduced generators and incorporates their capability profiles into model selection. VISTA [3] combines candidate tournaments with visual, audio, and contextual critique to refine prompts, while VQQA [228] 27 uses diagnostic questions to guide refinement. SCMAPR [110] verifies rewritten prompts against atomic requirements before generation. GenMAC [109] extends revision to prompts, bounding boxes, and guidance through specialist feedback. Beyond Trial-and-Error [229] combines semantic prompt revision with search over seed and guidance. Specialized controllers address particular conditioning decisions. MVAgent [104] constructs conditions across multi-shot trajectories, while CamPilot [96] focuses on camera-work control. PhyPrompt [230] produces physics-aware prompts, and DPP-GRPO [231] targets diversity and relevance in prompt rewriting. Editing & Repair. Editing and repair specifies changes to generated content or its underlying representation while seeking to preserve satisfactory parts of the result. VideoRepair [232] refines misaligned regions while protecting correctly generated content. PhysAgent [233] repairs executable scene-state and event programs after reconstruction and simulation checks. CutCraft [234] adjusts cut points, audio offsets, and transitions, with reported trade-offs between transition quality and within-shot synchronization. Crayotter [235] addresses sequences of semantic editing decisions, while Aurora [131] plans editing conditions for fixed video editor. These interfaces expose different correction units, with different preservation constraints and costs. 5.2.3 Memory & Experience Production decisions draw on information accumulated within project and across previous attempts. We distinguish Project Context from Retained Experience according to the role of the information being preserved. Project Context. Project context maintains the characters, references, and intermediate states with which subsequent production decisions must remain consistent. DreamFactory [236] carries character descriptions and preceding visual references through multi-scene production. CineAgents [126] verifies production blueprint against hierarchical source-film memory. Both make earlier information available for later planning and consistency checking. Retained Experience. Retained experience records previous actions and outcomes so that related decisions can draw on evidence of successful choices and recurring failures. AesopAgent [237] combines knowledge store with Experience-RAG, preserving feedback entries for workflow, prompt, and utility decisions. A2RD [238] stores successful and unsuccessful prompt rewrites with rubric scores, combining retrieval with hierarchical segment repair. EditDuet [128] retains scored and repaired communication examples for its Editor and Critic. Its collection-specific in-context examples support coordination, while cross-collection accumulation remains untested. 5.2.4 Skills & Reusable Procedures Production knowledge can be reused as shared guidance or as routines assembled for different requests. We examine these forms through Prompts & Production Rules, followed by Skill Construction & Composition. Prompts & Production Rules. Prompts and production rules encode shared instructions and constraints governing how stages are performed, reviewed, and retried. AESR [239] maintains strategies, templates, and pitfalls in prompting playbook alongside current-video repair. CineForge [240] represents production guidance through stage contracts, prompt rules, retry budgets, and review routing. AVA-Encoder [241] uses shared shot and keyframe encoding prompts for film reconstruction, separating reusable instructions from repairs to the current film knowledge graph. Skill Construction & Composition. Skill construction and composition packages production methods into reusable routines and combines them into workflows for different requests. SkillPE [242] constructs cinematic skill library from variants of expert seed skills inspired by film references. The selected library remains fixed during deployment. VideoWeaver [13] combines fixed foundation skills with category-level composition skills and creator skills for constructing further workflows. Its evaluation covers evolved composition skills and skill creators applied to unseen categories, extending reuse from production routines to the procedures that build them. Adaptation and Learning Across Components. Within-task adaptation refines the current production attempt through mechanisms such as prompt revision in VISTA [3] and workflow revision in VideoAgent [226]. Cross28 task learning instead retains updates for later use. Non-parametric approaches revise production rules in CineForge [240], shared encoding prompts in AVA-Encoder [241], and skill libraries in SkillPE [242]. Retention still requires independent validation: AESR [239] accumulates its playbook using test-set feedback. Parametric approaches optimize controller policies. VideoGen-Agent [5] combines supervised trajectories with GRPO, while NEWTON [222] uses trajectory-level Flow-GRPO. MultiMedia-Agent [220] applies staged supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization; Aurora [131] combines supervised fine-tuning with offline DPO. Specialized supervision includes shot comparisons in MVAgent [104], film-derived labels in CamPilot [96], video feedback in PhyPrompt [230], and text-space rewards in DPP-GRPO [231]. Crayotter [235] addresses credit assignment across editing stages. Deployment further supplies click-through preferences in AgenticGen [221] and interaction feedback in Recommendation as Generation [223]. Production experience can also inform development beyond the current request. The feedback collected by production systems becomes useful for model or harness improvement when it identifies which capability failed, under which conditions, and which intervention could address it. Retaining traces or preferences supplies evidence, but the effect on later development depends on how that evidence changes data collection, training objectives, or update selection. Persistent revision of the development harness extends this use of experience to the procedures that produce updates. VideoWeavers creator skills illustrate this direction within skill construction. Related work outside video generation includes Video-RSI [59], which evolves the harness of video understanding agents with frozen model weights, and the Darwin Gödel Machine [18] and RRSI [19], which revise agent code or harnesses across generations. For video generation, the mechanisms reviewed here support parts of such process, but do not yet establish that revisions to the development harness make successive rounds of generator development more effective. Section 5.3 examines the evaluation needed to assess both retained capability gains and changes to the improvement procedure.

sections.title: 5.3 Evaluation in Self-Improvement
sections.content: Evaluation supports progress toward RSI by providing feedback for proposing updates and independent evidence for assessing their effects. We distinguish two complementary perspectives: (i) Video Output Evaluation, which assesses video quality, task fulfillment, and observable failures; and (ii) Agent Harness Evaluation, which examines how the production system contributes to these outcomes, diagnoses failures, and carries out corrective interventions. For agentic video generation, identifying an unsatisfactory result is only the first step: useful feedback must help connect visual evidence to decisions or representations that the system can revise. Across both perspectives, development feedback should remain distinct from evidence used to validate improvements. Evaluation should also distinguish improvements to the current output, retained capabilities that benefit later tasks, and changes to the procedure that produces subsequent updates. 5.3.1 Video Output Evaluation Video output evaluation measures the properties of generated videos and identifies where they fail to meet requirements. We review four complementary elements: (i) Metrics and Benchmarks; (ii) Model-Based Judging; (iii) Human Assessment and Evaluator Reliability; and (iv) Agentic Evaluation Pipelines. Together, they specify what is tested, how it is measured, how judgments are validated, and how evaluation is executed. Metrics and Benchmarks. Metrics and benchmarks translate video capabilities into test cases and quantitative measurements. Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [243] measures distributional similarity between real and generated videos, but its sensitivity to visual content can obscure motion defects [244]. FVMD [245] instead measures motion through tracked points. VBench [246] and EvalCrafter [247] extend assessment to visual quality, temporal consistency, motion, and textvideo alignment. More targeted benchmarks operationalize specific capabilities: T2V-CompBench [248] evaluates compositional instruction following; VBench-2.0 [249] covers physical and commonsense plausibility; VideoPhy [250] and VideoPhy-2 [251] test physical interactions. StateBench [252], V2V-Bench [253], and AVGen-Bench [254] extend coverage to state consistency, sourcepreserving editing, and audiovisual generation, respectively. DirectorBench [255] extends evaluation to longform agentic production through structured checkpoints for script, visual, audio, cross-modal, and stability criteria. These measurements capture different properties: distributional fidelity, temporal consistency, and 29 successful execution of requested action should not be treated as interchangeable. Explicit world representations can provide additional reference information (Section 4.3). Agent-built worlds supply reference-backed evaluation sets for the Programmable World Model [161], Code Video Model [168], and SolarRenderer [158]. Specified objects, states, and events can support checks of whether generated content follows the intended structure. These references strengthen evaluation only to the extent that adherence is checked against the rendered video; the correctness of program alone does not establish the correctness of its visual realization. Model-Based Judging. Learned scoring models and LLM/VLM judges assess requirements that fixed summary metrics capture poorly. LLMs can decompose instructions into criteria, while VLMs inspect visual evidence. VideoScore [201] and VideoReward [14] learn scoring functions from human ratings or preferences. VideoBench [256] uses structured questions, while VideoScore2 [257] and AIGVE-MACS [258] combine scores with explanatory feedback. Rubric-guided evaluation makes criteria and scoring rules explicit: VideoArgus [259] constructs output-blind rubrics from the input, RewardVerse [204] learns rubric-based scoring, and RAVENEval [260] uses order-reversed pairwise comparisons to reduce position bias. Criterion-level judgments can identify unmet requirements, but an explanation of visual defect does not by itself establish its cause in the production process. Human Assessment and Evaluator Reliability. Human assessment provides supervision and reference for validating automated judgments. SafeSora [261] separates helpfulness and harmlessness, EvalVerse [262] incorporates filmmaking expertise, and PhyGround [263] uses observable physical criteria. Evaluator reliability concerns agreement with humans and sensitivity to errors: UVE [264] examines scoring and frame-sampling choices, Spotlight [265] tests error detection and temporal localization, and SLVMEval [266] introduces controlled defects into long videos. When judges also supply learning feedback, independent evaluation helps distinguish quality gains from reward overoptimization [267]. VideoGen-Agent [5] reuses its training judge and rubrics for automated testing, making its human comparisons important additional evidence. Dont Read the Log [268] identifies execution-log bias in the tested Qwen-VL judges, underscoring the need to inspect generated videos directly and specify the evidence available to each judge. Agentic Evaluation Pipelines. Agentic evaluation pipelines organize instruction analysis, evidence collection, and scoring into executable procedures. VideoGen-Eval [269] and VideoArgus [259] combine instruction analysis with specialized inspection tools, while VQQA [228] generates video-specific questions. Evaluation Agent [270] and Open Evaluation Agent [271] adaptively select prompts and tools. RAVEN-Eval [260] reduces comparison costs through selected reference generators. TEAR [272] and SceneSplit [273] extend testing to temporally structured safety failures. Prompt coverage, sampling policies, tool configurations, judge reliability, and evaluation cost jointly determine whether measurements are reproducible and informative. Active Testing [274] further highlights that adaptive test selection requires care when estimating overall performance; failure rates on deliberately adversarial prompts should be distinguished from those on representative requests. These measurements identify observable defects, but do not by themselves establish which production decision caused failure or how it should be corrected. The next perspective combines output evidence with plans, intermediate states, and execution traces to evaluate diagnosis and repair. Because repeated optimization can overfit particular tasks or judges, resulting gains should be checked on held-out requests with independent evaluation. 5.3.2 Agent Harness Evaluation Agent harness evaluation examines how prompts, memory, skills, tool interfaces, and control logic support video production and its improvement. We organize this assessment around four dimensions: (i) Effectiveness and Efficiency, which assesses performance gains and their costs; (ii) Diagnosability and Repairability, which examines whether failures lead to accurate diagnoses and effective corrective actions; (iii) Generalization, which tests whether gains extend beyond development tasks; and (iv) Continual Adaptation, which tracks progress and regressions across successive updates. The evaluation setting should specify what changes, what persists, and which feedback is available. Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents [275] compares four approaches: parallel sampling explores 30 independent trajectories under fixed harness; sequential refinement revises trajectories using previous attempts while keeping the harness fixed; harness evolution updates shared harness across tasks; and harness scaling revises the harness for an individual task. These settings differ in their update targets and scope of reuse. In video generation, VISTA [3] and VQQA [228] refine individual requests. Evaluating persistent harness changes additionally requires examining their effects on subsequent tasks. Effectiveness and Efficiency. Effectiveness concerns task completion, instruction fulfillment, and video quality; efficiency concerns the resources needed to develop and operate the harness. An agentic pipeline can improve on single generation call by sampling more candidates, revising the plan, or supplying better generation conditions. To attribute gains to harness revision, comparisons should control model and tool versions, match feedback access and resource budgets, and include fixed-harness sampling or refinement baselines. Ablations of plan revision and conditioning should use matched sampling budgets to distinguish their contributions from additional generation attempts. When script or plan is rewritten, the resulting video should be evaluated against the original user brief so that plan revision does not redefine task success. Controller training and generator upgrades should be evaluated separately where applicable. Resource reporting should include generator, critic, and controller calls, wall-clock time, and computational or monetary cost. Update-development costs should be reported separately from subsequent production costs. AFlow [276] reports performancecost comparisons, while SICA [277] evaluates accuracy, runtime, and monetary cost. Evo-Bench [278] records development-side progress and final held-out performance. MetaHarness [279] uses prior harness code, scores, and execution traces to inform subsequent proposals, illustrating how aggregate results can be supplemented with process evidence. In video generation, AgentMV [105] allocates generation resources under global budget constraint and evaluates the resulting qualitycost trade-offs. VideoWeaver [13] combines process and output assessment with human rankings and resourceuse measurements. VideoGen-Agent [5] includes fixed-tool training ablations and human comparisons; its generator-upgrade experiment separately measures the benefit of changing generation tools. Such comparisons help identify which intervention contributes to gain and at what cost. Diagnosability and Repairability. Evaluation should assess whether harness identifies actionable failure causes and corrects them while preserving satisfactory content. VideoRepair [232] illustrates regional correction, while PhysAgent [233] exposes scene-state and event programs as repair targets. Using shared failed outputs or controlled faults, comparisons with unguided retries and full regeneration should hold generators, tools, and resource budgets fixed, reporting diagnostic accuracy, repair success and locality, preservation of correct content, and recovery cost. Proposed causes should be checked through targeted interventions, since visual localization alone does not establish causal diagnosis. Generalization. Generalization assesses whether selected harnesss benefits extend beyond the tasks used to develop it. New examples from the development distribution test in-distribution generalization, while different task categories or domains test out-of-distribution generalization. The selected harness and its shared cross-task state remain fixed during this assessment. Prescribed within-task reasoning and repair may still operate, but test feedback should not drive candidate selection or persistent updates. GEPA [280] separates candidate selection on validation tasks from final testing, while ADAS [281] examines transfer across tasks and models. RRSI [19] evaluates evolved harnesses on other benchmarks. In video generation, VideoWeaver [13] tests frozen evolved skills on new cases and task categories, while VideoGenAgent [5] evaluates an unseen task combination. For diagnostic and repair mechanisms, generalization also concerns unfamiliar failure types and production configurations. Development-time validation can guide whether rule or skill should be broadly retained or restricted to category; final testing should remain independent of those decisions. Continual Adaptation. Continual adaptation assesses how harness performance changes over successive updates. Evaluation tracks whether additional experience improves performance, how quickly gains emerge, and whether later updates degrade previously supported capabilities. The task distribution may remain stable or change with production requirements and available tools. ACE [15] and Evo-Harness [282] use completed tasks to inform subsequent updates. EvoHarnessBench [283] distinguishes externally supplied harness expansion from experience-driven adaptation, showing that additional tools, skills, or agents can impair earlier-task performance even with fixed model weights. For video harnesses, evaluation should track quality, completion rate, and cumulative cost across updates, testing current and earlier task families for gains and regressions. 31 Repeated diagnosis-and-repair tests can additionally reveal whether the harness becomes more effective at correcting recurring failures. Stagewise adaptation should use data separate from evaluation; online evaluation should score each task before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. Together, these perspectives assess video quality, retained harness capabilities, and the ability to diagnose failures and verify repairs. Establishing RSI requires an additional comparison at the level of the development procedure ρk. fixed-procedure baseline and system allowed to revise its procedure should start from matched components and receive comparable feedback access and resource budgets. The retained procedural changes should then be used in subsequent development rounds, with independent tasks assessing the quality and cost of the updates those rounds produce. Evaluation should track whether the revised procedure produces better updates for given budget, reaches comparable quality at lower cost, and preserves earlier capabilities across repeated rounds.

sections.title: 6 Agent Design for Video Generation
sections.content: Agent design for video generation connects perceptual and reasoning capabilities with generation interfaces, feedback, reusable experience, and collaboration (Figure 8). The production, world-model, and improvement settings reviewed in above sections impose different requirements on this architecture. An isolated clip can often be produced through small number of model calls, while long narrative or continuing interaction can require persistent state, explicit controls, and recovery from partial failures. Reliable design allocates these mechanisms to the constraints that materially affect task success. Figure 9 organizes these five design aspects into their constituent dimensions and representative works. Perception, memory, and planning establish the information available to the controller; model invocation, coding, and GUI interaction determine how decisions are realized. Feedback governs assessment, recovery, and acceptance, while skill reuse and multi-agent organization influence how experience and responsibility are distributed. These design choices should be assessed through their effects on output quality, controllability, cost, and transfer across complete workflows. Together, these design aspects govern how video agent pursues goal through successive generation and revision decisions. At decision cycle t, the controller πϕ receives context ct assembled from the goal, current observations, and relevant production state. This state, st = (qt, mt, bt, et) in the formulation of Section 2, tracks task and artifact records qt, memory mt, remaining budget bt, and runtime records et. When generation is invoked, the selected prompts, references, and controls form the conditions supplied to the video generator pθ.

sections.title: 6.1 Foundational Agent Capabilities
sections.content: A video agent requires perceptual evidence, persistent state, and reasoning over interdependent decisions. These capabilities must accommodate temporal change, audiovisual correspondence, and uncertain generation outcomes. Their required granularity depends on the task: isolated clips may need little history, whereas long narratives and continuing interactions require selective access to earlier constraints. Omnimodal perception. Omnimodal perception interprets text, images, video, and audio to recover taskrelevant entities, events, relationships, and constraints. Source material defines what should be generated, while intermediate outputs reveal what has been realized. Application-specific systems emphasize source fidelity and creative intent [97, 98, 284286]; social and interactive settings additionally require interpreting preceding behavior and communicative context [224, 287, 288]. Perceptual state should distinguish requested properties, observed content, and uncertain inferences so that later decisions do not treat an assumption as an established fact. Cross-modal interpretation associates observations with shared entities and temporal intervals. Musical structure, lyrics, and beats can constrain shot duration and edit timing [102, 105, 289], while audiovisual production connects speech, expressions, subtitles, and background sound [85, 87, 290]. Correspondence does not always require simultaneity: voice-over, reaction shots, and off-screen events can intentionally separate sound from visible action. Geometric state and tool reports provide supplementary observations whose provenance should remain distinct from rendered evidence. 32 Figure 8: Agent design for video generation. Five design aspects surround shared video under construction. Foundational capabilities, environment interaction, and feedback-guided control support audiovisual production. Experience and skill reuse support adaptation, while multi-agent organization enables coordination. Scenes and timing are conceptual illustrations. The main design trade-off is perceptual coverage versus acquisition cost. Sparse frames and event summaries support many semantic checks, but short-lived motion defects and sound timing may require denser observations. Targeted questions, adaptive sampling, and criterion-specific inspection provide selective alternatives [228, 258, 259]. Evidence acquisition is most useful when it resolves uncertainty that can change generation, preservation, or acceptance decision. The controller should retain the source and temporal scope of each finding and revisit the media when compressed summaries cannot support the required judgment. Memory management. Memory management represents, updates, and retrieves the information needed beyond the current observation. Visual references preserve appearance, while structured records capture entity state, shot dependencies, accepted versions, and production history [2, 236, 291296]. Stable identities and locations must remain distinguishable from changing poses, clothing, viewpoints, and interactions [297, 298]. Multi-turn editing also requires retaining earlier changes and user preferences [299301]. Raw media offers detailed, traceable evidence; structured state and summaries reduce access cost but may omit information needed for later decision. Admission and updates require reliability checks because generated content can introduce errors into subsequent conditions. GroundShot [103], StoryMem [302], and Memento [303] illustrate selective verification or retention of references. practical memory should record whether an entry is source requirement, an accepted output, superseded version, or rejected candidate. Changes to reference should expose their downstream dependencies, allowing affected shots to be reconsidered while preserving unrelated accepted content. Retrieval constructs the context available to the next decision. Entity-indexed, semantic, spatial, and boundedhistory mechanisms offer different precisioncost trade-offs [143, 304312]. Model-side retention [313, 314] and sparse retrieval for video understanding [315318] provide enabling mechanisms. Extending general agent memory [319] to video therefore requires policies for selecting relevant evidence, compressing it without losing critical relations, and preserving provenance. Provenance and version records in mt and qt allow omitted evidence to be retrieved when later decisions require it. Long-horizon planning. sections.title: 6.2 Agent–Environment Interaction
sections.content: A video agent interacts with generators, reference stores, editors, renderers, and, in interactive settings, world model. Interaction can take the form of invoking task-level capability, constructing executable controls, or operating visible software interface. Ordinary model calls remain central: an agent can choose conditions, obtain candidates, and revise generation without writing code or using GUI. Interface design determines the control available to the agent and the evidence returned after execution. Model and tool invocation. Task-level invocation selects an available capability and supplies its inputs: text-to-video request, reference-conditioned shot, an editing operation, an inspection query, or world-model control. single generator is appropriate when it exposes the needed controls; additional models and tools can address limitations in identity, motion, sound, or editing. VideoGen-Agent [5] and MVAgent [104] illustrate policies that choose augmentation, generation, and reference operations. useful tool set exposes information gathering and candidate inspection alongside synthesis, enabling uncertainty to be resolved before an expensive commitment. Conditioning interfaces determine how much of the intended behavior can be communicated. Reference videos or image pairs can convey motion, physical behavior, perspective, and appearance transformations [327332]; context layout and efficient conditioning affect the cost of providing these signals [333, 334]. The agent must match the reference to the requested relation and preserve target-specific content. Fine-grained parameters improve flexibility but increase selection errors, while higher-level tools simplify reasoning at the cost of hidden internal choices. ComfyMind [335] illustrates composition through higher-level functional modules. Editing systems expose operations at different levels of abstraction, including semantic timeline changes and executable processing commands [124, 127129, 226]. Reliable invocation requires validated arguments, identifiable input and output versions, and recoverable asynchronous job state. For continuing world interaction, control must additionally be linked to the interval and state in which it takes effect. The interface should support checking both whether an operation completed and whether its output satisfies the task; the world-model settings are examined in Section 4. Coding and program execution. Coding constructs or revises the executable logic through which content is produced. Programs and declarative specifications expose geometry, timing, animation, and data relationships as variables and operations that can be inspected and changed. ComfyUI [336] provides an editable graph of executable nodes; scripting and graph construction offer different ways to compose such operations. The design choice is which properties require explicit control and which visual details can be delegated to neural synthesis. This is particularly consequential for precise event timing, physical layouts, and instructional content. GPT4Motion [337] and VideoCoCo [338] combine procedural dynamics with generative appearance synthesis. Editable blockouts in Scene2Scene [339], the fal workflow [340], and Seedances clay-reference interface [341] illustrate related uses of coarse spatial control with different degrees of human involvement. Scene and physics 35 methods expose inspectable conditions at the cost of construction and simulation [119, 121, 169, 222, 342, 343]. Executable teaching, data, and browser graphics support precise visual structure and timing [113, 114, 344349], with adjacent foundations in visual programming and graphics decomposition [350353]. hybrid workflow can retain precise structure in an executable scene program and delegate appearance synthesis to neural generator: pθ (cid:0) (cbase, Render(P )), z(cid:1). (14) Here Render(P ) supplies draft video or structural guide, while cbase contains the remaining conditions; together they instantiate from Section 2, with controlling sampling randomness. Neural refinement may alter geometry or timing, so the resulting video must be checked against the constraints encoded in . Execution should preserve the correspondence between program controls, runtime state, and rendered intervals. Errors and simulation traces expose process failures, while inspection establishes whether valid program achieved the intended result. Access to both the specification and final video supports targeted diagnosis, local editing, and reusable parameterized procedures. These benefits must justify the effort of constructing, executing, and checking the explicit representation. GUI-based software control. GUI control is valuable when required production operations are unavailable through stable programmatic interface or depend on inspecting the applications visible state. The agent observes previews, timelines, tracks, selections, and parameter panels and acts through mouse, keyboard, and shortcuts. General interface-control research provides relevant foundations [354358], while CutVerse [359] evaluates video-production applications. Temporal targeting is especially demanding: an apparently successful interaction can affect the wrong clip, track, or interval. GUI operations trade broad application coverage for sensitivity to layout, hidden state, and interaction history. Scrubbing and playback may be necessary to verify effects that static screenshot cannot establish. AssistEditor [360] illustrates combining visual and programmatic interaction. Hybrid execution can use direct tools for repeatable processing and the GUI for application-specific edits, provided asset versions, timecodes, and project state remain consistent across interfaces. Recovery should start from an observed state rather than assume that click or shortcut had the intended effect.

sections.title: 6.3 Feedback-Guided Agent Control
sections.content: Feedback controls whether an agent accepts result, gathers more evidence, corrects an artifact, or changes the remaining workflow. The measurements reviewed in Section 5 become operationally useful when they are attached to identifiable constraints and available interventions. Effective control distinguishes assessing result, diagnosing its failure, and deciding whether further effort is warranted. Evaluation and verification. Evaluation estimates perceptual quality and task fulfillment, while verification checks explicit requirements and execution conditions. Compiler or tool success cannot establish correct geometry, narrative fulfillment, or audiovisual timing. Fine-grained assessment and temporal localization provide evidence about content defects [255, 265, 361]; Evaluation Agent [270] illustrates adaptive evidence collection. Simulation state and executable predicates provide complementary checks for physics and animation [233, 362, 363], and rendering feedback can guide code revision [364]. The inspection procedure should match the requirement being tested. Cheap validity checks can prune unusable candidates before expensive multimodal review, while denser temporal inspection is justified for transient or relational errors. Findings should identify the relevant entities, intervals, criteria, and uncertainty. Learned critics can disagree or inherit model biases, so subjective goals and ambiguous cases may require human assessment. Feedback quality is best judged by whether it supports reliable acceptance or correction decisions, alongside its agreement with independent evaluation. Failure diagnosis and recovery. Diagnosis connects an observed discrepancy to plausible source: the request, reference, plan, program, generator configuration, or execution operation. SCMAPR [110] checks rewritten prompts before generation, whereas searching seeds and guidance settings can address failures not resolved by prompt revision [229]. Critics and revision loops connect different defects to subsequent interventions [3, 103, 109, 228, 296]. useful diagnosis must support an operation that the system can perform and distinguish uncertainty about the cause from confirmed failure evidence. 36 Recovery selects the smallest intervention likely to correct the problem while preserving accepted content. Options include local editing, regeneration, reference replacement, parameter adjustment, or revision of an upstream plan. Feedback from environment execution [365], rendered presentation artifacts [366], and creator preferences [224] complements visual critique. ReAct [9] and Reflexion [84] provide general foundations for using observations and retained feedback in later decisions. Local repair limits immediate cost but may leave faulty dependency intact; broader regeneration can address the cause while introducing new variation. recoverable accepted state and checks for collateral changes are therefore essential to either strategy. Acceptance and stopping criteria. Acceptance should be based on satisfied task constraints and sufficient quality evidence; stopping should also account for diminishing improvement, retry limits, latency, and remaining budget. Candidate tournaments and selective critique [3] can reduce assessment cost, while global allocation across segments [105] helps direct trials toward influential or difficult shots. Further inspection or generation is justified when its expected decision value exceeds its cost. Already accepted material should be reconsidered when relevant dependency changes, not merely because more sampling is available. Acceptance checks use the latest artifact and verification records in qt; stopping also considers the remaining budget bt and execution history in et. Budget exhaustion does not establish successful completion: the system should record whether it accepted the artifact, stopped with unresolved constraints, or escalated for user judgment. Pending operations must be completed or explicitly cancelled before closure. Hard requirements support explicit checks, while aesthetic goals may need bounded comparisons or human selection. Repeated critique without an achievable intervention is reason to change strategy or stop. Comparisons should report rejected candidates, incomplete tasks, and total generation and evaluation cost, so additional sampling is not attributed to better controller.

sections.title: 6.4 Agent Experience and Skill Reuse
sections.content: Experience can supply context for current inference, be consolidated into reusable skills, or support later policy updates. Building on the improvement mechanisms in Section 5, reliable reuse depends on what is retained, how the procedure is validated, and whether its assumptions remain valid in the next task. Skill acquisition changes available knowledge; packaging and deployment make that knowledge accessible to the agent and its tools. In-context learning. In-context learning uses supplied examples to adapt inference while keeping controller parameters fixed [367]. DreamRunner [200] illustrates planning from an example, while A2RD [238] contrasts successful and failed refinement cases. Contextual examples are useful when tasks change quickly, relevant precedents are available, or model weights cannot be updated. They are less dependable when retrieved cases omit critical conditions, conflict with the current request, or consume more context than the controller can effectively use. Examples in ct should preserve the task, the decision or procedure, and its observed result, allowing the controller πϕ to adapt its decisions while ϕ remains fixed. Memory supplies candidate records; the controller determines which relationships apply to the current story, shot, or tool choice. Evaluation should compare downstream outcomes with and without relevant examples under matched tasks, initial observations, available tools, generator parameters θ, and generation budgets. Length-matched irrelevant examples help distinguish useful experience from prompt-length effects. Following fixed instructions or replaying stored code alone does not establish adaptation from examples. Skill acquisition and refinement. Recurring solutions can be abstracted into prompting rules, tool-use procedures, parameterized programs, or generation workflows. ExpeL [368], Agent Workflow Memory [369], and Voyager [370] provide general precedents for extracting or retaining reusable knowledge. Video systems develop experience stores, model-specific playbooks, composition skills, and validated production updates [13, 237, 239, 240, 371]. Useful skills retain the input assumptions, asset requirements, operations, constraints, and failure cases that explain when the procedure works. Refinement should address recurrent failure patterns and be evaluated on tasks distinct from those used to propose the change. Broad recipes transfer more easily but leave execution details unresolved; narrowly tuned procedures can achieve stronger control while depending on particular models or tool versions. When stable decision errors require learned policy change, parameter training offers another mechanism [5, 208, 221, 223]. Its costs and benefits should be attributed separately from improved retrieval or reusable instructions. Retaining earlier capabilities after each update is as important as improving the latest task. Skill packaging and deployment. deployable skill combines procedural guidance with the resources and checks needed to execute it. The Agent Skills specification [372] illustrates package containing SKILL.md file with metadata and instructions, plus optional scripts, references, and assets loaded as needed. This can express shot-construction procedure, blockout-to-video workflow, or editing routine. Parameterized programs are useful when timing, geometry, and local-edit controls must remain explicit. The package should identify its dependencies, supported inputs, and expected outputs; its format alone does not establish learned competence or transfer. Skills supply knowledge about when and how to use capability, whereas tools expose executable operations. MCP [373] standardizes tool discovery and invocation through declared argument schemas. Comfy Skills [374] packages workflow guidance and commands, while Comfy MCP [375] exposes workflow discovery, execution, and output retrieval. Deployment must reconcile the skills assumptions with available nodes, models, assets, parameter semantics, and permissions. Tests on new tasks and after tool or generator changes should establish both portability and retention, including whether the resulting video still satisfies the skills acceptance checks.

sections.title: 6.5 Multi-Agent Organization
sections.content: Multiple agents are useful when specialization, parallel work, or independent review compensates for the cost of routing information and synchronizing state. single controller can remain preferable when dependencies are tight and the required tools fit one context. Team design must establish who is responsible for task, what information collaborators share, and how competing assessments lead to an accepted result. Task delegation and team composition. Delegation assigns collaborator task, relevant context, permitted changes, and an expected deliverable. Role-based video systems [85, 87, 376] organize specialized production components, while FRAMEWORKERS [92] illustrates dynamic routing as tasks and available capabilities evolve. Fixed roles simplify accountability for stable workflows; dynamic teams accommodate heterogeneous requests but introduce routing and context-selection errors. Studies of agent scaling, routing, and pruning [377 379] motivate selecting team size according to task demands rather than maximizing the number of agents. , c(i) ), where identifies the collaborator, g(i) delegation request can take the form at = (delegate, i, g(i) its subgoal, and c(i) its scoped context. The request must belong to the currently admissible action set At and respect its permissions and budget constraints. Runtime records et link delayed results to their requests, preserving task ownership until the returned artifacts are verified and incorporated into shared state. ComfyUI-based systems distinguish the team that constructs workflow from the graph that executes it. ComfyAgent [380] uses cooperating agents to construct workflows, ComfyGPT [381] specializes agents in reformulation, graph construction, refinement, and execution, and ComfyMind [335] combines modular composition with planning and feedback. Their evidence concerns general generative-workflow construction; applying these organizations to video also requires temporal and audiovisual assessment. computation node is not an independent decision-maker merely because it belongs to graph. Video-oriented projects also use the term agent swarm. FilmSwarm [382] describes director-led preproduction pipeline with dynamically instantiated specialists, shared references, and roundtable deliberation; its documented deliverables include video production plan. SwarmZeros Livepeer video-generator example [383] coordinates script, scene, image, video, editing, and upload agents through manager. These project and documentation examples establish integration patterns rather than controlled evidence of decentralized intelligence or improved final-video quality. Swarm configurations need explicit delegation and communication policies, and should demonstrate gains over single controller with comparable tools and budget. Shared-state coordination. Collaborators need consistent asset identities, accepted shot versions, temporal constraints, and dependency records. Shared specifications and persistent state [6, 105, 384] reduce repeated context reconstruction but require clear ownership and update propagation. Typed media references [104] preserve details that prose can omit. Parallel slide, scene, or shot production [296, 346, 385] is most effective when outputs can be checked against stable shared conditions; coupled changes to the same state may require sequential execution. An accepted update should identify which downstream tasks must revisit their inputs. 38 Communication format should preserve the information needed by the recipient. Text and structured artifacts support inspection and broad compatibility. LatentMAS [386] and Vision Wormhole [387] explore latent message interfaces with compatibility or alignment requirements. Shared world representations in WorldWeaver [388] and OmniDrive [389] couple generated viewpoints rather than production-role decisions. Their relevance lies in how information is preserved and propagated; improved coordination must still be measured in the target workflow. More detailed messages help only when recipients can use them without excessive context and communication cost. Collaborative review and decision-making. Collaborative review distributes the assessment of proposed plans or artifacts and returns actionable feedback to the responsible component [89, 109, 128, 390]. Independent perspectives can expose overlooked errors, but correlated critics and repeated debate may increase cost without improving judgment. Reviewer assignments should specify the criterion, affected content, required evidence, and authority to recommend or accept change. clear decision rule is needed when agents disagree, particularly for subjective creative goals. Useful review produces verifiable revision or an explicit acceptance decision. Critiques should preserve the relation between the observed defect and proposed intervention, while the reviser reports what changed and what was retained. The shared state is updated after checking the revised result against the relevant constraints. Evaluation should compare independent review, manager arbitration, and other decision procedures at matched budgets, including latency, unresolved disagreement, and collateral changes. Escalation or termination rules are necessary when further discussion cannot resolve the task. Effective video agents combine control precision with selective use of computation. Explicit representations are valuable where geometry, timing, or content must be inspectable; richer observations are valuable where uncertainty can change decision; and reusable skills or collaboration are valuable where recurring procedures and separable responsibilities justify their overhead. The resulting architecture should make accepted state, failure evidence, resource use, and retained improvements traceable, allowing system-level benefits to be distinguished from stronger generators or additional sampling.

sections.title: 7.1 Fully End-to-end Video Production
sections.content: Fully end-to-end video production means autonomously turning an initial idea into complete film or television episode through scriptwriting, audiovisual design, asset creation, generation, editing, and final delivery. The target is finished work that meets commercial requirements for quality, continuity, and delivery, without relying on repeated human prompting and revision. The agent harness must coordinate dependencies, allocate resources, and recover from tool failures across this pipeline. Critic feedback should link specific failure to an actionable repairfor example, revising plan, replacing reference, regenerating shot, or re-editing sequencewhile preserving accepted content. DirectorBench [255] finds transitions between units to be the lowest-scoring part of current long-form workflows (Section 5.3), highlighting the need to assess continuity across unit boundaries. Acceptance and stopping criteria grounded in the original creative intent and available budget remain undeveloped, leaving the harness without reliable basis for deciding when further revision is warranted and when the production is ready for delivery.

sections.title: 7.2 Lifelong Memory
sections.content: Autonomous agentic video generation and sustained world interaction require agents to maintain stable, persistent memory across shots and interaction sessions. Generated frames alone do not necessarily provide dependable record of character identity, object properties, scene changes, or completed events, especially when these facts leave the current field of view. StoryMem [302] conditions later shots on dynamically updated visual memory, while WorldMem [143] retrieves memory frames together with associated states to reconstruct previously observed scenes. These mechanisms provide foundations for continuity, but lifelong memory should also preserve useful experience beyond single generated sequence or simulated episode. future agent harness should distinguish project specific records, such as accepted character references and 39 event histories, from transferable experience, such as successful tool configurations, repair strategies, and reusable production procedures. The challenge is not simply to store more context, but to retrieve relevant evidence, update records when the project changes, and discard obsolete or unreliable information without losing established constraints. Memory entries should retain their provenance, temporal scope, and artifact versions so that the agent can distinguish verified outcomes from unconfirmed plans. Evaluation should test whether retained experience improves new projects and revisited environments, while controlling for additional context and avoiding transfer of conflicting identities or outdated assumptions.

sections.title: 7.3 Hybrid Code-Pixel Generation
sections.content: Hybrid code and pixel generation combines programs that represent scene state and controllable dynamics with video models that synthesize the resulting imagery. Code supplies explicit object, camera, and interaction constraints, often through rendered proxy frames, while the learned generator adds appearance and motion detail, so programmable structure and pixel synthesis jointly determine the video. Programmable scaffolds offer promising foundation: the World Narrative Model [169] uses an editable physical representation to guide video synthesis, while PhysAgent [233] combines executable physical programs with simulation, verification, and repair. These approaches make generation conditions inspectable and editable rather than expressing them only through prompts. Code and rendered proxy videos already serve as persistent scaffolds shared by an agent and generator in recent engineand program-driven renderers (Section 4.3), but each is typically trained for one structural representation, only some run in real time, and their paired data come from small number of engines. The Genie 4 announcement [391] explicitly identifies hybrid world models as future direction, combining structured reasoning by code and language models with pixel level simulation. It describes closer integration of Gemini for scene structure and narrative planning with Genie for audiovisual simulation as an early step toward this goal. Video generators and world models could further expose callable code interfaces for querying state, updating entities, specifying events, controlling cameras and actions, and advancing the simulation. The agent would maintain structured state, translate its updates into supported generation controls, and verify whether the resulting video realizes those updates. key challenge is keeping program state, agent memory, and generated observations aligned: executing command or storing an object record does not guarantee that the generator preserves its consequences. The interface must therefore support both explicit intervention and verification of its effects, allowing the agent harness to preserve accepted state and correct deviations over extended generation and interaction.

sections.title: 7.4 Autonomous Human-free Development
sections.content: The same autonomy should extend from producing videos to developing the models that produce them. longer term goal is an agent harness that independently diagnoses model weaknesses, acquires or constructs relevant data, designs training experiments, executes updates, evaluates candidates, and retains or rejects changes without manual intervention in each iteration. Failures from agentic video generation and trajectories from world interaction could supply evidence for this development loop, allowing the system to identify missing capabilities and generate targeted supervision. Achieving RSI, however, requires more than automating fixed sequence of data collection and training. Improved capabilities must also strengthen the procedures used to discover failures, select data, design interventions, and validate subsequent updates. The agent harness should therefore be able to revise development code, experiment strategies, and reusable improvement procedures using evidence from earlier rounds. Major challenges include attributing gains to specific interventions, preventing errors in generated supervision from accumulating, coordinating updates to generators and critics, and preserving earlier capabilities. Among these, the one through which an evaluator selects data and accepts updates is the most exposed, because video development relies mainly on learned judges. Independent validation and recoverable model versions are necessary to determine whether autonomous iterations produce durable progress rather than adaptation to the systems own evaluation signals.

sections.title: 7.5 Efficiency
sections.content: Efficiency concerns the quality and scale of finished work that system can deliver under fixed time and resource budget. Review loops add generator, critic, and controller calls, failed attempts, and wall clock time, yet these quantities are rarely reported under common accounting protocol. common accounting, reported alongside quality, would make it possible to compare multi-agent pipeline with single long-context generator and to judge whether an improvement round was worth its cost. The agent harness should allocate resources across generation, inspection, and repair, reuse accepted assets and intermediate results, and decide when further refinement no longer justifies another call. Comparisons should account for all attempted operations, including rejected candidates and verification, rather than reporting only the final generation. For model development, cumulative data, training, and validation costs must also be tracked across update rounds.

sections.title: 7.6 Provenance and Safety
sections.content: Agentic production multiplies the operations applied to single asset. shot may be generated, locally regenerated, edited, re-timed, and composited by different tools before delivery, and mark or credential attached at one step does not necessarily describe the result of later ones (Section 3.5). harness already records which tool produced which artifact; extending these records into signed provenance for every accepted version, as C2PA Content Credentials [140] do for edits, would make the history of delivered video auditable. Identity references raise related question that current systems leave to the user: whether person whose likeness is stored as an asset consented to its reuse across projects, and how harness should enforce such limits. Safety should cover both generated content and the operations used to produce it. The agent harness should bind reuse permissions to identity assets, check generated and edited outputs against content restrictions, and enforce access and execution limits on production tools and generated code. These constraints should follow assets across derived versions and projects, so that an edit, tool change, or memory reuse cannot bypass an established restriction.

sections.title: 7.7 Emerging Tasks
sections.content: Agentic video generation could enable new tasks in which video creation, interactive experience, and iterative development are parts of the same workflow. Automated game creation is one promising example. GameNGen [142] demonstrates action conditioned simulation of an existing game, and GameGen-X [148] supports generation and interactive control of game videos. Building on such capabilities, an agent harness could coordinate narrative and level design, asset generation, gameplay code, audiovisual synthesis, and automated playtesting, using observed failures to revise the resulting experience. However, generating visually playable trajectories is not equivalent to authoring complete game. The system must also establish explicit rules, persistent state, success and failure conditions, and reproducible interactions, and verify that visual outcomes agree with the intended mechanics. Other prospective tasks include interactive storytelling that adapts to audience actions, personalized audiovisual learning environments, and scenario generation for testing agents in simulated worlds. These tasks shift the objective from delivering fixed sequence to maintaining coherent experience whose content changes in response to participants. They also connect the three directions of this survey: agentic video generation constructs the audiovisual content, video world modeling supports interaction, and model development could address limitations revealed by repeated use. These tasks require benchmarks for complete video systems, not just isolated outputs. Existing evaluations remain largely centered on generated video quality or the capabilities of individual video models. Recent benchmarks cover parts of the problem. DirectorBench [255] diagnoses long-form generation workflows, WorldScore [174] and PlayWorld [8] test world models over sequences of generation or interaction, and harnessevolution studies [275, 283] compare updated and fixed harnesses on general agent tasks. None of them yet measures, for video, whether the agent harness can autonomously complete an entire production workflow, maintain persistent state across extended generation and interaction, recover from failures, and improve system capabilities through successive development rounds. Agent orchestration also creates opportunities to 41 extend video duration and support richer narratives, more characters, and more complex event dependencies. Benchmarks should therefore measure the generation horizon and content complexity that complete system can sustain under explicit quality, consistency, and resource constraints, rather than evaluating only predefined clips. Progress should be evaluated through task completion, controllability, persistent consistency, and development cost, in addition to visual quality. For RSI, evaluation must additionally track gains, regressions, and cumulative costs across multiple updates, using independent tasks to test whether improvements persist and transfer. Comparisons should establish whether an evolving system becomes better at producing subsequent improvements, rather than benefiting from additional sampling, stronger tools, or repeated training.
